> Although they used to pray for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists, when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it. So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers

**A PRAYER ANSWERED AND THEN REFUSED**

The verse recalls a hope the community had carried for generations and the way it behaved when the hope was granted: ***“Although they used to pray”***, ***“for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists”***, ***“when there came to them a Book from Allah”***, ***“which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it.”***, ***“So may Allah's condemnation be upon the disbelievers”***. They had asked for a victory that would come through a prophet, and they had described his coming as their own vindication; the prophet came, the Book came, and their answer was the reverse of their prayer. What the verse adds is that they recognized it, so the refusal was not the result of a misunderstanding about which message had arrived. The confirmation of their own scripture is named as evidence in the sentence, since the Book that came confirmed what they already held and gave them no ground for surprise.

**RECOGNITION AND WHAT CAME OF IT**

The Book uses the vocabulary of recognition deliberately, and it uses it again in a passage where those who were given the scripture are described discarding the new revelation as though it were merchandise: (2:101 — **“Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—confirming”**). The same image of a people who can identify the truth and then refuse it runs through the sūrah's account, and the psychology is not unusual. A person can recognise a claim as true and still reject it because accepting it would rearrange his position, and the Book presents this community as the clearest case of that condition in its own history. Anyone who has seen a person accept a fact and then act against it has watched the same behaviour at a smaller scale. The verse records it at the level of a nation so that the pattern is unmistakable.

**WHEN THE ANSWER BECAME A GRIEVANCE**

A prayer for victory had long been part of how this people understood itself, and its fulfilment through a prophet of another nation turned the hope into a grievance. The covenant to acknowledge the messenger is recalled in another sūrah, which shows how old the arrangement was: (3:187 — **“˹Remember, O Prophet,˺ when Allah took the covenant of those”**). What the community wanted was the victory rather than the one through whom it would arrive, and the verse exposes the difference between the two desires. The same difference is available to any reader who has prayed for an outcome and then found the means of it inconvenient. Nothing here suggests the prayer was insincere; what the sentence establishes is that the answer did not arrive in the shape the askers had imagined.

**THE STUDENT WHO WILL NOT WRITE THE ANSWER**

Think of a student who has spent a term predicting the question that will appear on the examination, and who sees it on the paper and cannot bring himself to answer it because the answer is not the one he had prepared. A scripture was already in these people's hands, describing the messenger's coming, and the messenger's arrival made the description an obligation rather than a comfort. The Book's phrase about recognition removes the possibility that the refusal was honest confusion, and it leaves the community with a choice they had made in full knowledge. A reader who has been waiting for a particular thing to happen can ask himself what he would do if it happened through a door he does not like. The answer is what the verse is designed to test.

**A PRONOUNCEMENT AT THE CLOSE**

The sentence that closes the verse is a pronouncement rather than a description, and the Book uses that form when the conduct has been established beyond doubt. The community's prayer is set beside its refusal, and the verdict follows from the two facts in the same sentence. The chapter's argument does not rest on the verdict alone, since everything before it has been laid out for the reader to examine, and the reasoning is laid out so that a reader can follow it rather than accept a conclusion. What makes the passage useful is that the same pattern can be reproduced in a person's own life in a single week: a request made in earnest, an answer that arrives with a condition, and a decision taken quietly against it. The Book records the pattern at the scale of a nation and leaves the reader with the smaller version of it.

**PRAYER AS A MEASURE OF WHAT A PERSON IS WILLING TO RECEIVE**

The verse teaches something about the difference between wanting a result and wanting the truth, and it does so without any commentary of its own. The community's long prayer had become a slogan that no longer described what its speakers wanted, since a prayer for victory through a prophet is a prayer to be led by him. A reader can apply the test to the requests he makes most often, and he will find that some of them include conditions he has never spoken. The Book's account here is one of its clearest illustrations of that gap, because the community had stated the condition in advance without noticing it. What this refusal produced is traced in the verses that follow, and the sequence shows a people defending a position they have stopped examining.

---

## Verse 2:90

> Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for—denying Allah’s revelation and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants! They have earned wrath upon wrath. And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment

**WHAT WAS SOLD, AND FOR WHAT**

The verse puts the whole matter in commercial language and then states what was sold and why: ***“Miserable is the price they have sold their souls”***, ***“for denying Allah's revelation”***, ***“and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants!”***, ***“They have earned wrath upon wrath.”***, ***“And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment”***. The deal is called a sale of the self, a phrase that makes the goods and the buyer one and the same person. Two motives are named in the same sentence, and the second is the one that explains the first: the objection was not to the content of the revelation but to the recipient of God's favour. The clause about grace being given to whom He wills is the Book's answer to the whole dispute, since the community's grievance was about a decision that was never theirs to make; the same sentence is carried in a later sūrah for this people: (3:112 — **“They will be stricken with disgrace wherever they go,”**).

**ENVY AS THE MOTIVE BEHIND A THEOLOGICAL OBJECTION**

The Book names resentment of divine grace as a motive in several places, and it treats the feeling as candidly as it treats the deed. A later sūrah raises the same question and answers it with the same reference to God's freedom to give: (4:54 — **“Or do they envy the people for Allah's bounties? Indeed,”**). The point is not that the community had no arguments; the point is that the arguments were assembled after the conclusion. When a person's objection to a message is really an objection to the messenger's standing, the reasoning he produces will never be satisfied by evidence, and the Book's account here shows the mechanism at work on a national scale. Anyone who has seen a decision dismissed for the standing of the man who proposed it will know this pattern, and the passage's interest is in how such arguments are generated rather than in the arguments themselves.

**WRATH UPON WRATH**

The verse describes the consequence in a phrase that doubles what a reader would expect, and the doubling is explained by the sequence of the story. One layer of anger belongs to the rejection of the messengers and the covenant, and another belongs to this refusal of a Book the community had recognised, so that the accumulated account grows with each opportunity that is declined. The Book's habit of describing consequences as accumulated rather than instantaneous is worth noticing, since a reader often assumes that a single act is being answered. The later verses in this sūrah describe a community that resists through several stages, and the Book tracks each stage in the same sentence as its cost. What this means for a reader is that the account of his own conduct is also cumulative, and no single decision stands alone.

**THE TRADER WHO REFUSED THE CONSIGNMENT**

Think of a merchant who has waited years for a consignment, who refuses it at the dock because the shipping agent is from the wrong family, and who then explains the refusal with a story about quality. The consignment had been awaited for generations and was inspected closely enough to be recognised, and it turned it away for reasons that had nothing to do with the goods. The Book's verdict names the humiliation that follows, and the humiliation is not arbitrary; it is the natural end of a position that cannot be defended in the open. Anyone who has seen a group argue itself into a corner for the sake of standing will find the closing words of this verse already visible in the argument. The Book states the outcome plainly so that the pattern can be recognised while it is still in progress.

**THE HUMILIATION THAT CLOSES THE VERSE**

The last clause names a specific kind of punishment, and the choice of humiliation rather than pain is connected to the offence. A community that had been motivated by standing lost standing, and the Book records the correspondence instead of leaving it to the reader. The chapter arranges consequences in this way often, shaping each one after the deed that earned it: the people who traded guidance for error were traded in return, and the people who raised themselves were brought low. Read as one passage from the covenant onward, the account holds together, and its final clause is the last entry in a long ledger rather than a bolt from nowhere. The verse closes on humiliation, and humiliation is the mirror of the envy that produced the refusal.

**AN ACCOUNT OF ONE'S OWN**

The passage teaches that the account of a community's conduct is kept in the same language as its motives, and the same ledger is open to the reader's own audit. A person who resents another's success will dress his objection in principles, and the history of this people shows where that road ends. The remedy is not to suppress the feeling but to notice it, since the objection the community made was answered and the answer did not help them. A reader who wants to use the verse can begin by naming the last time he dismissed a piece of information because of who delivered it, and then checking whether the information was true. That exercise is what the passage asks of a reader, and nothing further needs to be said about it.

---

## Verse 2:91

> When it is said to them: “Believe in what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,” and they deny what came afterwards, though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures! Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Why then did you kill Allah’s prophets before, if you are ˹truly˺ believers?”

**A SWORN LOYALTY TO HALF A REVELATION**

The verse reports the answer this community gives when it is invited to believe, and the answer is a formula: ***“When it is said to them”***, ***““Believe in what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,””***, ***“and they deny what came afterwards”***, ***“though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures!”***, ***“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Why”***, ***“then did you kill Allah's prophets before”***, ***“if you are ˹truly˺ believers?””***. The claim to believe in what was sent down to them is used as a reason to refuse what came later, and the Book points out that the later revelation confirms the earlier one rather than contradicting it. The sentence then turns the claim into a test by reaching into the community's own history, since the prophets sent to them had been killed by some of the same people who now describe themselves as believers. A profession of faith that survives only its own documents has been placed under examination.

**THE LOGIC OF A CLOSED CANON**

The community's position has a recognisable shape: what was given to them is authoritative, and anything arriving after it is not. The Book's answer does not dispute the authority of the earlier scriptures; it points to the connection between the two revelations, which is confirmation rather than replacement. A passage later in the sūrah describes the same people discarding what came to them while holding on to what they had, and the act is described there in the terms of something cast aside: (2:101 — **“Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—confirming”**). The problem with a closed canon is not the reverence it shows toward a text but the authority it quietly takes for itself, since deciding that revelation has ended is itself a claim about God's speech. The verse exposes that claim by pointing to the conduct of the community that made it.

**REACHING INTO THEIR OWN PAST**

The closing question is the sharpest instrument in the passage, because it tests the profession against the record. If they believe in what was sent to them, then the prophets who came with that same message were their own, and the killing of some of them was not the act of believers. The Book's habit of using a community's history against its self-description appears throughout the sūrah, and it is a method rather than a rhetorical flourish. A reader who has heard a group define itself by its loyalty to a tradition can ask what that group has done with the people who carried the tradition, and the answer is often an embarrassment. The question in this verse does not need an answer; it needs only to be asked in the presence of the record.

**A COMPARISON WITH A FAMILY THAT KEEPS THE PHOTOGRAPHS AND NOT THE INSTRUCTIONS**

Think of a household that keeps its grandfather's photograph on the wall and has lost the letter it wrote about the family's conduct, and whose members invoke his name to settle arguments they never actually consult him about. The earlier scripture was in these people's possession, along with a claim to believe in it, and the claim was being used to refuse the continuation of the same message. The Book's answer is to point at the parts of the inheritance that had been quietly set aside, which is a test any family or community can run. The verse does not accuse the whole people of killing prophets; it accuses enough of them to make the profession hollow, and the Book's language throughout the passage is carefully distributed. What this sentence leaves behind is a measure: loyalty to a tradition is tested by behaviour toward the people who carry it.

**WHY NO COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS GIVEN**

The passage records the community's words and then answers them with a question rather than a counter-argument, and the choice is deliberate. The Book treats the claim about the earlier scriptures as self-evidently inconsistent with the conduct it names, so no long rebuttal is needed. The same method was used earlier when the community was asked about its own covenant, and it shows how often a plain record is allowed to do the work of an argument. Anyone who has read from the covenant onward can supply the rest of the reasoning himself, which is precisely the effect intended. What remains is the question, and it is left standing over the community's profession like a witness who has not been dismissed.

**HOW LOYALTY IS MEASURED**

For a reader of the page, the verse offers a way to test his own attachment to what he has received, and the test is not about documents but about conduct. A person can accept the revelation he was given and still refuse the parts of it that inconvenience him, which is the offence the preceding verses described. The Book's answer in this verse is to name the historical fruits of that habit in the community that practised it, so that the reader sees where the path leads over generations. A community that has decided the era of correction is over has also decided that its own arrangements cannot be questioned, and the Book's question can be asked of it at any time. The verse ends with the question unanswered, and the reader is the one who is expected to answer it.

---

## Verse 2:92

> Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully

**THE CALF THAT FOLLOWED THE CLEAR PROOFS**

The previous verse asked a question about the community's history, and this one answers it with a single event: ***“Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs”***, ***“then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully”***. The proofs and the calf are placed in the same sentence, and the order is the point: the signs came first, and the worship of the image came after. The Book does not say the community lacked evidence when it built the idol; it says the evidence had already arrived and the idol was made anyway. The word at the end describes the act as a wrong done by the actors themselves, and the Book keeps that attribution in the sentence rather than offering it as commentary. A reader who has been following this passage from the covenant to the messengers now sees the pattern stated in its plainest form.

**THE PROOFS THAT CAME BEFORE THE FALL**

The calf has already appeared earlier in this chapter, where a visible god was demanded during the prophet's absence on the mountain and the demand was answered as a trial. What this verse adds is the summary judgement on the whole episode, and the judgement is that the wrongdoing belonged to the people rather than to the circumstances. The Book repeatedly makes this move in its accounts of the past, because a reader is always tempted to look for conditions that explain a failure away. The generation that made the calf had seen the sea split and the water come from stone, and it still needed something it could see standing in front of it. A reader who has decided that he would believe given enough evidence can measure himself against that record.

**THE ABSENCE OF MOSES AND THE PRESENCE OF A SUBSTITUTE**

The verse names the prophet's absence as part of the scene, and the detail is worth noticing because every generation produces its own version of it. When the leader is away, the community's attachment to the message is tested, and an object that can be carried out of a tent becomes very attractive. The Book's account in another sūrah describes the making of the idol from the jewellery the people had taken out of Egypt, which ties this failure to the wealth they had carried along with their freedom. The substitution is the same today in communities where the leader's image replaces his teaching, and where a movement keeps its momentum after the message has been set aside. The verse's single sentence contains that entire history in the two clauses it arranges.

**A CREW THAT FOLLOWS A CAPTAIN, NOT A CHART**

Think of a crew that has been given a chart and a course, and that stops following the course the moment the captain goes below deck, and that then argues about which direction the ship should point. Clear proofs had already been given, which are the chart of the metaphor, and it turned to an image as soon as the man who had carried the proofs was out of sight. The Book's judgement is that the wrong was theirs, which is the same conclusion every reader reaches about such a crew. A person who has built his practice around a person rather than a teaching is in the position described in the verse, and the test arrives on the day the person is not there. The remedy is not to distrust leaders but to hold the message as the thing that carries them.

**TWO FACTS A READER MUST HOLD TOGETHER**

The sentence is a conclusion drawn from the history that precedes it, and it prepares for the verses that follow, where the community is asked why it kills prophets if it truly believes. The Book's arrangement therefore asks the reader to hold two facts together: the proofs that were given and the conduct that followed them. A reader who has received a great deal of guidance and settled into a comfortable practice can test himself on the same two facts, and the test does not require a mountain or a sea. The Book's language here is deliberately plain, and its plainness is the reason the passage works on a reader who has read it many times. The next verse returns to the covenant and to the answer the people gave when they were bound by the mountain.

---

## Verse 2:93

> And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and obey,” they answered, “We hear and disobey.” The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do, if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!”

**TWO WORDS GIVEN IN REPLY TO A COVENANT**

The pledge is renewed and the reply is reported without softening: ***“And when We took your covenant”***, ***“and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to”***, ***“that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you”***, ***“and obey,” they answered, “We hear”***, ***“and disobey.” The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts”***. The answer is a sentence that sounds like acceptance and ends in refusal, and the Book quotes it whole because the shape of the sentence is the shape of the community's condition. The command had asked for two things, holding and obeying, and the reply keeps the first half and discards the second. The same words are recorded again in a later sūrah as a saying of this people, which shows that the phrase was remembered as part of their own speech rather than invented by an accuser: (4:46 — **“Some Jews take words out of context and say, “We listen”**).

**FOUR WORDS AND WHAT THEY CONCEDE**

The reply is remarkable for its honesty, since a community that meant to deceive would have said only the first word. What the Book reports is a group of people who know exactly what is being asked and who state their position in the plainest available form. The early teachers read the pair as an admission that the mountain compelled an outward agreement rather than an inward one, so that the second word explained the first. That reading fits the scene recounted above, where the mountain was held overhead and the agreement was extracted under a weight. The verse therefore records a decision taken in full view of the terms, and the reader who has watched a person agree to something while making clear he will not do it has the same transaction in front of him.

**A HEART IN WHICH THE CALF HAD TAKEN ROOT**

The clause that follows explains the answer, and it uses the language of growth: ***“The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts”***, ***“because of their disbelief”***. The image is of something planted that has spread, and the Book dates the planting to the episode in the wilderness when the image was made and worshipped. A later passage describes the consequence in the same vocabulary, connecting the covenant-breaking with a hardening that followed it: (5:13 — **“But for breaking their covenant We condemned them”**). The two answers were therefore consistent with each other, since a heart occupied by the calf had no room for the command that forbade it. The order of the two words matters: love of the calf is given as a result of disbelief, so the sequence runs from refusal to affection, not the reverse.

**A CLOSING ADDRESS TO THE CLAIMANT**

The same charge, of a covenant honoured in words while the messengers who carried it were killed, is laid elsewhere in exactly those terms: (5:70 — **“Indeed, We took a covenant from the Children of Israel and sent them messengers.”**). The sentences here end with an address that turns the community's own claim against it: ***“because of their disbelief. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do”***, ***“if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!””*** The claim is not denied; it is examined, and the examination is done by the community's own conduct. If the scripture in their hands was what they said it was, the conduct it would prompt should look different from the killing of prophets and the worship of a calf. A reader who has heard a claim of loyalty measured against the fruit it produces will recognise the method, and the Book uses it here without a single additional argument. The question is the last word of the verse, and it is left where the reader can pick it up.

**AN APPLICATION THAT ANY COMMUNITY CAN RUN**

The passage is not only about one people's history, since the sentence it examines is available to anyone: agreement in words while the intention goes the other way. Think of an employee who accepts a policy in a meeting and describes the same policy as absurd over lunch, or a congregation that recites the creed and treats the obligations that follow as optional. The Book's report of this answer is valuable precisely because the answer is so short, and short sentences reveal what longer ones conceal. A person can take the last occasion on which he said that he had heard a command and ask whether the second half of that sentence was also true of him. What the verse records is what such a test looks like when it is conducted in the open.

**WHENCE THE CONFIDENCE CAME**

The community's confidence in its own position is the last thing to notice here, since the claim about the Torah is made by people whose conduct is being described in the same verse. The Book treats that confidence as a symptom rather than a strength, and it does so because the claim had become a shield for the conduct. The chapter's earlier verses have shown the same arrangement in other forms, where a doctrine about a short punishment made repentance unnecessary and a claim about an exclusive future supported a comfortable present. What this verse adds is the mechanism: a person can hold a scripture in his hands and let it stand for the obedience he has not given. The Book's question interrupts that arrangement by asking what the belief actually prompts, and the answer is left for the reader to supply.

---

## Verse 2:94

> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity, then wish for death if what you say is true!”

**TESTING A CLAIM OF EXCLUSIVE SALVATION**

A claim of this kind was not unique to one community, as a later passage shows when it is reported in the words of both peoples at once: (2:111 — **“The Jews and Christians each claim”**). The verse takes the claim about the next life and turns it into a wager that can be settled at once: ***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively”***, ***“for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity”***, ***“then wish for death”***, ***“if what you say is true!””*** The claim is not denied in this verse; it is accepted for the sake of the argument, and then a consequence is drawn from it. A person who is certain that he is going to a permanent home with God, and who has been told that the waiting period is a hard one, ought to want the waiting to end quickly. The Book asks for the wish rather than the death, because a wish cannot be performed as a show. The sentence is a test of sincerity that requires nothing but a person's own desire, which is why it is such an uncomfortable form of proof.

**THE ONE ACT THAT CANNOT BE FAKED**

The Book could have asked for an oath or a sacrifice, and it asks for an interior act instead, and the choice is instructive. A wish for death is a statement about what a person expects to find, and it cannot be made sincerely while the expectation is absent. The community had been claiming an exclusive share of the next world, and an exclusive claim that leaves the claimant desperate to remain here is a contradiction that anyone can see. Another passage puts the claim about the Garden to the same kind of test, and the practice here is to let a claim carry its own examination. What the reader learns from the technique is that a doctrine about the future can be tested by the shape of a person's desires in the present.

**ORIGINS OF A CLAIM ABOUT THE GARDEN**

The claim was not an isolated eccentricity; it was a settled self-understanding that had grown over generations, and it appears twice in this sūrah in different forms. The Book reports the community asserting a limited punishment for itself in one place and an exclusive Garden in another, and the pattern shows a doctrine built to secure a position rather than to describe a fact. A later passage addresses the same confidence with the same invitation, so the reader meets the argument more than once: (62:6 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O Jews!”**). What an inherited claim of this kind protects is not usually a belief but a manner of living, and the Book's test reaches past the claim into the life that the claim was shielding. A reader who belongs to a community with a settled story about its own standing can hear the same question asked of him.

**DEATH AS A MEASURE OF WHAT A PERSON EXPECTS**

Think of a man who has been promised a house in a better country and who has spent thirty years finding reasons to postpone the voyage. The Book uses the wish for death as a lens because it measures expectation without allowing the usual evasions, and the measurement is uncomfortable for anyone who has not examined his own hope. The verse does not condemn the desire to live; the sūrah praises life and forbids its destruction elsewhere. What it exposes is the gap between a stated certainty about the next world and the actual preferences of the person stating it, and the gap is available to any reader who is honest. The Book's question in this verse is not answered by its hearers, which is an answer in itself, and the next verse explains why.

**A TEST THAT REQUIRES NOTHING BUT HONESTY**

The invitation in this verse is an unusual kind of proof, since it costs the person nothing to perform and cannot be performed falsely. Anyone who has read from the covenant up to this point can see the whole method of the sūrah in one sentence: a claim is stated, a consequence is drawn, and the conduct of the claimant is allowed to speak. The Book's interest here is not in extracting a confession but in showing a community the shape of its own position, and the demonstration is complete before anyone answers. What the reader takes away is a way of examining his own hopes, since the test can be adapted to any claim about the future that a person makes. The next verse supplies the result, and the result is given before the community has a chance to reply.

---

## Verse 2:95

> But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers

**THE WISH THAT WAS NEVER MADE**

The Book supplies the answer before anyone speaks, and the demand that produced it stands in the verse just before this one: (2:94 — **“then wish for death”**). What the challenge produces is a refusal: What the challenge produces is a refusal: What the challenge produces is a refusal: ***“But they will never wish”***, ***“for that because of what their hands have done.”***, ***“And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers”***. The test asked for a wish, and the verse reports that the wish will not be made at any time, which makes the absence of the answer into the answer. The reason given is not a doubt about the next life but the record of what the people have already sent ahead of them, and the Book names their own hands as the source of the reluctance. The last clause then states that this record is fully known, so the reader understands that the reluctance is not a hidden motive discovered by an accuser but a fact about the people themselves.

**WHY AN UNCLEAR ACCOUNT MAKES A MAN HESITATE**

The phrase about hands is the Book's regular way of describing accumulated conduct, and here it explains an emotion rather than assigning a penalty. A person who suspects that his account is not in order will not ask for it to be brought forward, and that is the condition the verse describes. The same reasoning appears in the sūrah's earlier warning about the Day when no soul can help another, where the emphasis falls on what each person has carried to that meeting. The confidence these people held about the next life was evidently never a confidence about their own record, and the two could be held together only while nobody asked the question plainly. The test in the previous verse was chosen because it forces those two things into the same sentence.

**A KNOWLEDGE THAT LEAVES NOTHING OUT**

The closing clause is short and it does two things at once: it states that the wrongdoing is known, and it quietly declines to describe the people as anything else. The Book uses this formula wherever a conduct has been established beyond dispute, and it uses it at the end of verses that a reader might otherwise treat as a debate. Here the clause also protects the reader from the impression that the challenge was a piece of rhetoric which the Book won by default, since the reason for the silence is given in the same breath. A reader who has ever kept quiet when a question would have required an honest answer has the mechanism in front of him, and the mechanism is being described as something God already sees.

**A MAN WHO WILL NOT READ HIS OWN STATEMENT**

Think of a partner in a firm whose books have been called for and who finds reasons why next year would be a better time. The verse's phrase about hands is the call for the books, the refusal to wish is the postponement, and neither step requires the firm's accounts to be set out in the passage. The point of the passage is that a person's reluctance is itself information, and the information is available to anyone watching. A reader can test the same thing in himself whenever he avoids a question that would require him to state his position clearly, since the avoidance usually has a reason attached to it. The verse names the reason and then leaves the reader with it, and the next verse shows how far the reluctance can go.

**WHAT AN UNANSWERED CHALLENGE SHOWS**

The verse is one of the Book's clearest demonstrations of a claim being tested by conduct rather than by argument, and the demonstration works because the silence is total. The community had an opportunity to settle the matter in its own favour with a single sentence, and the Book records that the sentence would never be spoken. Anyone who has seen a confident assertion collapse the moment it required a commitment has watched the same structure at a smaller scale. No further verdict on the claim is required, since the conduct of the claimants has done that work already. What remains for the reader is to notice the places in his own life where a similar test would produce a similar silence, and the next verses continue the description of what this community preferred to the wish they were invited to make.

**THE PREFERENCE REVEALED BY RELUCTANCE**

The verse leaves the reader with a portrait of a people whose attachment to the present was stronger than their confidence about the future, and the Book does not soften the diagnosis. That attachment is not unusual, and the account of those who traded the next life for this one has already covered the same ground. What makes this passage distinct is the way the preference is exposed: not by an accusation but by an invitation that the people declined to accept. The reader who notices how much of his own behaviour is shaped by not asking certain questions has understood the verse, and the Book's placement of it here, immediately after the covenant and before the account of magic that follows, shows that the whole section is about the difference between a claim and a life.

---

## Verse 2:96

> You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years. But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment. And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do

**A GRIP ON LIFE TIGHTER THAN ANYONE'S**

The Book keeps a separate sentence for those who reject the revelation outright, and this verse describes the appetite that holds them here: (64:10 — **“As for those who disbelieve and reject Our revelations,”**). What follows turns the reluctance of the previous sentence into a picture of desire: ***“You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years.”***, ***“But even if they were to live”***, ***“that long, it would not save them from the punishment.”***, ***“And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do”***. The comparison is striking, since the community is placed ahead of every other people in its attachment to this world, and even ahead of those who worshipped other gods. The thousand years names the shape of the wish rather than a number anyone expected to reach, and the Book then removes the comfort the wish was meant to secure. What the passage describes is a desire so strong that it becomes visible to an observer, which is why the verse opens with a command to look rather than with a report about belief.

**THE COMPARISON WITH THE POLYTHEISTS AND WHAT IT MEANS**

The Book had every opportunity to make this an attack on the community's religion, and it makes its comparison in the language of appetite instead. A polytheist believes in no reckoning to come, so his attachment to the present is entirely rational within his own view; a people who claimed an exclusive share of the next world should have been the least attached to this one. The Book's observation is that the actual order is reversed, and it states the reversal plainly. Another passage makes the same contrast, reminding this community of the favours it received and of how little the recipients gave in return. Anyone who has seen a group profess a future hope while clinging to present arrangements will recognise the portrait, which is offered without a single theological argument attached.

**THE THOUSAND YEARS AND THE LIMIT OF THE WISH**

The wish for a thousand years is the Book's way of describing a desire that wants more of the same rather than something better, and the phrasing quietly exposes the imagination behind it. A person who expected to be taken to a better place would not ask for a longer stay in the transit camp, and the wish in this verse asks for exactly that. The Book then removes the benefit the wish was intended to buy, since a longer life does not postpone the meeting and does not diminish the account. The same logic runs through the sūrah's treatment of spending and loss elsewhere, where what is kept back turns out not to be kept at all. What the verse teaches is that the length of a life is not the measure of what the life is worth, and the wish for length says something about the wisher rather than about his prospects.

**THE GUEST WHO WILL NOT LEAVE THE WAITING ROOM**

Think of a traveller who has been told that a room is prepared for him, and who spends the night in the airport lounge asking for the flight to be delayed. The Book's picture of this community is the same figure written at the scale of a nation, and the wish for a thousand years is the request for one more day in the lounge. The verse does not say that the community disbelieved in the promised room; it says the preference for the lounge was visible to anyone who looked. A reader who has been offered something better than his present arrangement and has quietly asked for more time will recognise the posture, and the Book's command to look at it is addressed to him as much as to the people of the verse.

**AN APPETITE THAT CANNOT BE HIDDEN**

The verse's opening verb is about observation, and the Book uses it because this condition cannot be hidden for long. A person's attachment to the present leaks into his decisions, his spending, and the risks he will not take, and a community's attachment shows in the arrangements it defends. The closing clause states that God sees what such people do, which places the observation made by any bystander on a firmer footing than a bystander could claim. What the reader should take from the verse is a way of reading conduct rather than a verdict on a people, since the appetite it describes is available to anyone who has been given a claim about the future. The next verse turns to the Angel who brought the revelation, and the community's objection to him, which is the same reluctance in another form.

---

## Verse 2:97

> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers.”

**AN OBJECTION TO THE ONE WHO BROUGHT IT**

The quarrel is closed in the next verse by naming every party at once, so that the objection to one messenger becomes an objection to them all: (2:98 — **“Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel,”**). The verse answers the quarrel with a messenger by describing what the revelation does: ***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know”***, ***“that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah's Will, confirming what came before it”***, ***“a guide and good news”***, ***“for the believers.””*** The objection behind the verse is not stated, and the Book does not need to state it, since the reply identifies the accusation precisely enough: the community had made the identity of the angel a reason to reject the message. The answer rephrases the whole affair in terms of function, and the functions listed are four: the revelation came down, it was placed in the heart, it confirms what came earlier, and it guides and gives good news. A quarrel about a name is answered with a description of what the named one has actually done.

**THE BEARER, THE HEART, AND THE PURPOSE**

A messenger's identity is not a trivial matter, since trust in the message depends on knowing who carried it and what kind of act the carrying was. The Book therefore does not dismiss the question; it answers it by naming the bearer, the destination, and the purpose in one sentence. The destination is named as the heart, which is where belief is formed and where the community's hardness had already been located earlier in the sūrah. The same constellation of ideas returns in the verse that follows this one, where the angels are named one by one and enmity toward any of them is answered in the same breath. A reader who has refused advice because of its source can see the Book's method here, since the message and the messenger are treated as parts of one act rather than as separate issues.

**CONFIRMATION AS THE ANSWER TO SUSPICION**

The revelation is described as confirming what came earlier, which is the strongest available answer to a community that already possessed scriptures. A revelation that confirmed their own books could not have been rejected on the ground that it disagreed with them, and the Book has already made this point several times in the sūrah. The naming of guidance and good news does the rest of the work, because these are the things a reader needs and the things the message claims to provide. Nothing in the verse defends itself with a miracle or an argument from power; the defence is a description of function, and the function is addressed to the community's own stated needs. That technique is used wherever the Book is accused of something, and it is why the answer here feels final despite its brevity.

**THE PATIENT WHO DOUBTS THE CHEMIST**

Think of a person who needs a medicine and refuses it because he does not like the pharmacist who prepared it. The Book's answer to the community in this verse is to name what the preparation contains and what it does, which is the only relevant consideration for anyone who needs the medicine. The angel's standing is not diminished by the community's dislike, and the revelation's contents do not change because the hearer was expecting another messenger. The reader who wants to apply the passage can ask whether he has ever rejected a piece of information on the ground of its carrier while knowing that the information was sound. The Book's handling of the objection shows what such a refusal looks like when it is examined, and the examination is what the verse performs.

**THE STATE OF THE ARGUMENT**

The sentence settles the dispute for anyone who is willing to weigh functions rather than reputations, and it leaves the objector with the option of continuing to refuse on grounds that no longer concern the message. The Book's placement of the verse here, after the account of a community's reluctance to part with life, shows that the two objections belong to the same disposition. A person who does not want the message will find a reason in the messenger, and the Book removes that reason without asking the person to like the messenger. What the reader takes away is a way of separating a claim from the person who delivers it, and the practice of that separation is the beginning of fairness. The next verse deals with those who extend the enmity to God and the angels together.

---

## Verse 2:98

> Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers

**AN ENMITY THAT TAKES IN EVERY MESSENGER**

The reply widens until it has gathered everyone the objection might touch: ***“Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel,”*** and, in the same sentence, Michael, so that the list ends with a verdict rather than a negotiation. The verse does not argue that Gabriel deserves better treatment; it places him inside a company that includes God, the angels, and the messengers, and it makes hostility to any member of that company a single position. The complaint had been about the identity of a courier, and the answer turns that question aside: the courier was never the issue, since the message came from the same source that sent every other message. The verse closes with its own verdict, and the naming of Michael inside the same sentence leaves the community's preference with nowhere to stand: ***“and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers”***. The angels are servants of the message here, and a quarrel with one of them is settled by the sentence that follows the list. The report carried from Ibn ʿAbbās places the verse over exactly this claim — one angel held to be a friend of the people, another held to be their enemy — and the answer was to put both names inside one sentence with the messengers and with God. What the community had been treating as a preference about staff is reclassified in one sentence as a stance toward the whole household.

**THE REPORTED OCCASION AND THE TWO ANGELS**

The accounts of how this passage came down agree on the shape of the objection, and one report traces it to a claim that Gabriel was the community's enemy while Michael was its friend. The two names are placed together in the verse precisely because the community had separated them, and the separation is what the Book refuses. The explanation given for the preference was that one angel was associated with severity and the other with rain and mercy, which turns an angelic office into a personal grievance about the weather. The account these people gave of themselves is visible here: they accepted the messengers whose business they liked and rejected the one who had carried the message it did not want. The verse removes the ground for that arrangement by refusing to let any of the named parties be treated as optional.

**WHY ENMITY WITH AN ANGEL IS NOT A SMALL MATTER**

Angels in the Book are described as servants who carry out what they are commanded, and hostility toward one of them is therefore hostility toward the order it serves. The same logic applies to the messengers, who are named in the list even though no one had accused them in this exchange. The verse treats a preference among servants as a decision about their master, and the closing words state the consequence in the plainest possible form. The reader who has heard someone praise a religious authority while despising the message that authority carried will recognise the pattern, and the Book's answer to it is a list rather than an argument. The list is short, and it closes the door on the idea that a person can hold the sender and reject the sending.

**ONE HOUSEHOLD AND ITS PICKED SERVANTS**

Think of a family that welcomes the gardener, tolerates the cook, and refuses to acknowledge the driver who brought the letter from the head of the house. That line had been drawn by these people, and the answer names the whole household in one sentence so that it cannot be drawn again. The point is not that every servant is equally prominent; it is that they are all sent, and the sending is what the objection was really about. A reader who has dismissed a piece of news because he disliked the person who brought it will find the argument here addressed to him. The verse does not ask for affection toward a courier; it asks the reader to stop treating his own preferences as a test of who deserves to be heard.

**LOYALTY DECIDED ALL AT ONCE**

The sentence leaves the community with no position except the one it has taken, since enmity toward the whole company is what the objection amounts to once its parts are named. The Book's habit of listing the parties in full is a way of preventing a dispute from being kept small, and the reader sees the technique at work here. A person who refuses the revelation on the ground of the messenger's identity has, by the same act, decided something about God, and the verse says so without raising its voice. What remains for a reader is the practical question of whether he has ever allowed a dislike of the carrier to settle his view of the message, since the Book treats that as the beginning of the position described here. The next verses return to the community's record of covenant-breaking, which the objection was being used to cover.

---

## Verse 2:99

> Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations. ˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious

**CLEAR SIGNS AND THE PEOPLE WHO DENY THEM**

The verse answers the claim that no evidence had been given, and it answers with a declaration: ***“Indeed,”***, ***“We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations.”***, and then with a description of the only people who deny them. The claim of the community had been that nothing recognisable had arrived, and the answer is that the signs were clear enough to be seen and that the denial comes from another source. The verse names that source with a single word, and the word describes a person who has stepped outside the bounds rather than one who has failed to understand. The reader is left with a picture of evidence on one side and a decision on the other, and the Book puts the two in the same sentence so that the second cannot be mistaken for a problem with the first.

**THE WORD FOR THE REBELLIOUS**

The term used here belongs to the vocabulary of boundaries, and it describes someone who has left the path rather than someone who never saw it. The Book uses the same word for those who break their agreements and for those who take what has been forbidden, so the emphasis falls on deliberate departure. A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās ties the verse to an exchange in which a man told the Prophet ﷺ that nothing recognisable had come, and the answer is that the signs were in front of him. A reader who has argued with a person about evidence and found that more evidence changed nothing has seen the same condition at a smaller scale. The Book's diagnosis is that denial of this kind is a choice about conduct rather than a verdict on proof.

**THE IDENTIFICATION OF THE DENIERS**

The sentence never suggests that people deny the signs because they are difficult; denial is restricted to the rebellious, which is a statement about who the deniers are. That is a harder claim than it looks, because it removes the ordinary excuses in advance and leaves the reader with a category. The Book makes similar identifications in other passages where the object of denial is named as conduct rather than as information, and the pattern is consistent across the sūrah. The reader who wants to use the verse without becoming a judge of others can apply it to himself, since the only denial he can examine from the inside is his own. The Book's interest here is not in labelling a community but in showing what the label describes, and the description is a decision to leave a known path. The same restriction of denial to the rebellious is repeated elsewhere in the Book, where the word is attached to those who have broken the terms they accepted, which is why the chapter keeps returning to covenants.

**THE DRIVER WHO MISSED THE SIGNPOST**

Think of a driver who has missed a turning and who tells his passengers that no sign was ever placed on the road, when the sign was passed at speed while he was looking elsewhere. Clear revelations had been given, the objection was that nothing recognisable had arrived, and the answer names attention rather than evidence as the missing item. The comparison is not flattering, and the Book does not intend it to be. A reader who has ever explained away a piece of guidance he did not want to follow can see how the explanation is constructed after the decision rather than before it. The verse names the construction and leaves the reader with it, and the naming is the whole of its remedy: a person who has been told that he looked away has been given something he can act on, unlike a person who is told that the evidence was never there.

**THE SIGNS THAT WERE ALREADY IN THEIR HANDS**

One thing the passage fixes is that the community being addressed was not without material, since the confirmation of their own scriptures had already been named several verses earlier. The signs in this verse are therefore not an unrelated display; they are the arrival of what the earlier books had described, which is why the denial is described in terms of rebellion. Someone who has been given a great deal and has chosen not to look will find the sentence aimed at him, and nothing here softens it. What the verse offers as a remedy is not stated here, and the next verses supply it in the account of what this community does with its covenants, which the reader can compare with his own record. The chapter's method is to keep the material and the conduct in view at the same time, and this verse is one of its clearest examples.

---

## Verse 2:100

> Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside? In fact, most of them do not believe

**COVENANTS THAT KEEP COMING APART**

The chapter returns to the community's record and states it as a question: ***“Why is it that every time they make a covenant,”***, ***“a group of them casts it aside? In fact,”***, ***“most of them do not believe”***. The pattern is described as repeated rather than exceptional, and the participle used for the people who discard the agreement shows that the discarding had become a habit rather than an incident. The Book does not ask why one covenant failed; it asks why every covenant fails, which moves the discussion from a single event to a disposition. The final clause gives the reason, and the reason is not forgetfulness or confusion. A community that does not believe in the thing it is promising to do will break the promise as a matter of course, and the Book states this before the reader has a chance to look for a softer explanation. The same conduct is described in a later sūrah for a generation that inherited the scripture and treated its terms as negotiable: (7:169 — **“Then they were succeeded by other generations”**).

**PROMISES MADE AND PROMISES REPEATEDLY SET ASIDE**

The verse is careful about which pledges are in view, and the distinction is worth holding on to. Some agreements in this history the community denied making at all, and others were acknowledged even as they were being set aside, and the Book addresses both in the same sentence. The covenant to make the scripture known, and not to hide it, is named in another passage with the same verdict attached, so the reader can see the charge repeated where the obligation is spelled out: (3:187 — **“˹Remember, O Prophet,˺ when Allah took the covenant of those”**). What the verse establishes is that the record of this people cannot be explained by a single failure under pressure, since the pattern outlasts the pressures that produced it. A community that keeps leaving its agreements has said something about what it takes them to be.

**WHY ONLY A GROUP IS NAMED**

The sentence names a group rather than the whole people, and the precision is significant for a reader who is tempted to turn the passage into a verdict on a nation. The Book's accusations in this sūrah are consistently measured in this way, and the same care appears in the verse that follows, which speaks of some of those who were given the scripture. The qualification matters: what is being described is a tendency inside a community rather than the identity of every member. A group that discards its agreements is enough to produce the reputation, and the account of how this people treated its prophets has already shown how a position held by a few becomes a public one. The reader's use of the passage is to examine whether he belongs to the group being described.

**A TENANT WHO SIGNS WITHOUT READING**

Think of a tenant who signs a new lease every year and treats the terms as a formality that has never been enforced, and who is surprised when the landlord finally acts on a clause. Agreements had been made here and set aside repeatedly, and the question suggests that the repetition had become invisible to the people doing it. The closing clause explains why: an agreement is only as strong as the belief behind it, and where belief is thin the paper is treated as decoration. A reader can run the same test on the promises he makes in the ordinary course of his life, since the Book's interest in this passage is in what a person's repeated conduct says about the value he places on his word. The verse asks the question and leaves the reader to find his own case in it.

**THE HABIT AND WHAT IT REVEALS**

The last clause of the verse supplies the diagnosis, and it is stated as a fact about most of the community rather than as a suspicion. Unbelief is treated here as the soil in which covenant-breaking grows, and the people's own account of their hearts has already appeared earlier in the sūrah. The verdict falls on people who accepted something and then treated their acceptance as negotiable, not on those who never accepted anything at all. The Book's language about belief is consistently about what a person's conduct shows, which is why a broken agreement counts as evidence in this passage. The next verse names the specific occasion that had provoked the question, and it shows what the community did when the messenger it had been promised finally arrived.

---

## Verse 2:101

> Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—confirming their own Scriptures—some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they did not know

**A BOOK CAST BEHIND THE BACK**

The verse names the specific occasion behind the question and describes how the community received what it had been waiting for: ***“Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—confirming”***, ***“their own Scriptures—some of”***, ***“the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah”*** behind their backs, and the Book adds that they did so as though they did not know. The messenger arrived confirming what they already held, and the response was to discard the confirmation as an item of rubbish. The gesture in the verse is worth pausing over, because it is the gesture of a person who wants something out of the way rather than something to be refuted. Nothing in the sentence suggests an examination of the messenger's claims; the Book records a movement, and the movement is away from the evidence. What the community did with the confirmation is stated in its own closing clause, and the clause is the Book's judgement on the whole gesture: ***“as if they did not know”***.

**THE GESTURE AND WHAT IT MEANS**

The phrase used for the discarding describes an object thrown behind the back, which is the posture of a person who intends never to look at the thing again. The Book uses the same image elsewhere for people who treat a scripture as an encumbrance, and it uses it here for the people who were its custodians. The clause about acting as if they did not know is a comment on the shape of the refusal rather than on their information, since the same community had been described in earlier verses as recognising what had arrived. The reading handed down from Ibn ʿAbbās describes a deliberate forgetfulness here, and it fits the verse's placement after the account of covenants discarded as a habit. A reader who has seen a group quietly shelve a report it had commissioned will recognise the motion.

**THE CONFIRMING THAT MADE THE REFUSAL STRANGE**

The messenger's arrival is described as confirming the community's own scripture, which means the new revelation did not ask them to abandon anything they held. The Book has already made this point several times in the sūrah, and it returns to it here because the refusal has now become an act rather than a debate. The same charge is laid out in another passage where the covenant to make the scripture known is joined to the account of what was hidden: (3:187 — **“who were given the Scripture to make it known to”**). A reader might reasonably ask what could be objected to in a message that agreed with the books already in hand, and the answer is supplied by the whole section: the objection was to the messenger and to the community that would receive him. The confirmation made the refusal harder to justify rather than easier.

**A FIRM THAT BURIES ITS OWN REPORT**

Think of a company whose auditors report exactly what the accounts show, and whose directors respond by filing the report and never mentioning it again. The confirmation of its own scriptures was in these people's hands, and the document was treated as an inconvenience to be put out of sight. The comparison is uncomfortable because the report is the only item in the story that could have settled the argument, and the Book records what was done with it. A reader who has watched an institution receive the evidence it asked for and then stop discussing the question has seen the same movement performed on a smaller stage. The verse names the manoeuvre and leaves the reader to notice where he has seen it.

**EVIDENCE ARRIVES AND IS SET ASIDE**

The passage settles an old question about the value of proof by showing what a community does when the proof arrives, and the answer has nothing to do with the quality of the proof. The Book's account is that the evidence was recognised and discarded in nearly the same breath, which is why it appends the remark about acting as though they did not know. A reader who has spent time trying to settle a religious question with arguments should notice what the verse assumes: that the barrier in the cases described here was never the argument. The next verse turns to a different subject, the magic that this community was said to have followed, and the transition shows the Book moving from what people refuse to what they prefer. What remains from this sentence is the gesture, and the gesture is the part a reader can check in himself.

---

## Verse 2:102

> They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon. Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved. They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon. The two angels never taught anyone without saying, “We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.” Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife; although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them—although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter. Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew

**THE ART THEY TOOK UP INSTEAD**

The verse begins by naming what the community had been doing while the confirming Book lay behind its back, and the first words set the alternative in place: ***“They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon.”***. The ˹instead˺ in the translation marks a substitution, as though a choice had been made between two available things, and the choice was made in favour of an art that the devils themselves had promoted. The period the verse names is the reign of Solomon, which places the practice in a time the community remembered as its own golden age rather than in some foreign or forgotten era. A report carried from Ibn ʿAbbās describes the community's claim in this connection as one that traced the art back to that reign, and the verse corrects the attribution in the same breath that it records the practice. What the reader is being shown is a people that had something better in its hands and reached for something else.

**SOLOMON IS CLEARED BEFORE THE STORY IS TOLD**

Before anything is said about what was taught, an accusation that had attached itself to a prophet is removed, and the removal is emphatic: ***“Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved.”***. The order of the two clauses matters, since the denial is placed first and the true subject of the charge second, so that the reader hears the correction before the deed is described. The Book has already shown, earlier in this sūrah, how a people's own traditions can dishonour the prophets it claims to honour, and the pattern repeats here in a single sentence. The historical claim that this king had commanded the art is traced by Ibn ʿAbbās to a story the community itself circulated, which means the verse is correcting an inherited slander rather than answering an outside critic. What stands after the correction is the true account of the art's transmission, and the transmitters are not the king but the devils who claimed it.

**THE TRANSMISSION AND ITS RECIPIENTS**

The sentence continues with the activity of those devils and names the recipients: ***“They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon.”***. The construction is worth a second look, because the revelation to the two angels is placed in the same clause as the teaching of magic, and the Book is careful to distinguish the two in what follows. Babylon is named as the place, and the naming gives the practice a location and a history rather than leaving it as a vague menace. The setting is the same city the community remembered as the site of its own exile, and a report from Ibn ʿAbbās places the two angels' descent there with a warning attached. A reader who has seen how quickly a practice acquires a respectable lineage will notice what this verse does with the lineage it is offered: it separates the divine revelation from the human art and refuses to let them share a name.

**THE WARNING THAT CAME WITH THE TEACHING**

The verse then reports the terms on which the knowledge was delivered, and the terms turn the whole episode into a test: ***“The two angels never taught anyone without saying,”*** and then the words they never omitted: ***“We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.”***. The disclaimer is spoken by the teachers themselves, which means the people who took the art up had been told plainly, at the moment of receiving it, what it was for and what it risked. There is no suggestion in the sentence that the information was unavailable or hidden, and none that the buyers were misled about the price of the transaction. The verse makes the two angels witnesses against the very use their knowledge was put to, and Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have read the clause as a warning rather than an invitation. What the reader should see is a decision made in the open, with the outcome stated in advance by the people who knew most about it.

**A PATIENT WHO READS THE WARNING LABEL**

Picture a patient who reads the leaflet that comes with a medicine, understands the risk it sets out, and takes the dose anyway because the effect is what he wants. The next words of the verse describe exactly that decision and its result: ***“Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife;”***, and the harm named is domestic rather than spectacular. The art's first effect is to split what the Book has spent much of this sūrah binding together, and the phrase marks the damage as reaching the smallest unit of the community. Ibn ʿAbbās describes the practice in this period as one that set spouses against each other, and the verse's own report of it is that it worked in exactly that way. Anyone who has seen a household come apart over something that promised an advantage to one of its members has seen the mechanism described here, and the Book is not finished with the subject.

**THE LIMIT ON THE HARM THEY COULD DO**

The following clause places a boundary around the whole practice: ***“although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will.”***. The art that the community had taken up, then, was neither self-sufficient nor secure, since the harm it produced was always within the permission of the One who permitted no other power. The same boundary appears in another sūrah where the claim of the magicians is measured against what God does with it: (10:81 — **“Allah will surely make it useless”**). The Book never treats magic as a rival power; it treats it as a technique that works inside limits, and this clause is one of the clearest statements of that position. A reader who has feared such things more than he feared God has the verse's correction in the sentence, and the correction is not so much a warning as a description of where the power actually lies.

**THEY TRADED SOMETHING FOR NOTHING**

The verse then states the bargain from the buyers' side: ***“They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them—”***, and the verdict is followed by a clause about knowledge that leaves no room for ignorance: ***“although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter.”***. The transaction described is one in which the purchaser knew the price and the loss before he paid, which places this community in the same family as the buyers of guidance named earlier in the sūrah: (2:86 — **“These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world”**). The Book's account of the episode is therefore about a settled decision rather than a seduction, and the sentence repeats the point about knowledge to keep that fact in front of the reader. What the people acquired here was a technique with no lasting use, and the clause about the Hereafter makes the accounting explicit rather than implied.

**THE SUM PAID FOR THE ART**

The verse closes with a verdict on the terms of the sale and then with an exclamation that leaves the reader holding the loss: ***“Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls,”*** and then ***“if only they knew”***. The word for the price suggests a measure that anyone could inspect, and the Book's judgement is that the sum was pitiful for what it bought. The final clause returns to knowledge, which the verse has already stated the buyers possessed, so that the exclamation reads as a lament over a knowing choice rather than a comment on information that never arrived. The passage has therefore come full circle from its opening: it began with a community following an art instead of a revelation, and it ends with the price of that decision stated in the plainest terms. The reading carried from Ibn ʿAbbās treats the closing exclamation as a lament over a knowing choice, and the verse's own words support him: the buyers had been told what the art was and what it cost. The next verse names the alternative that had been available the whole time, and the reader can compare the two outcomes for himself.

---

## Verse 2:103

> If only they were faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah, if only they knew

**THE CONDITION THEY NEVER MET**

The verse that closes this stretch turns from what the community did to what it might have had, and it opens with a wish: ***“If only they were faithful”***. The word for faithfulness here carries the sense of holding to something with confidence, and the Book places it first, before any mention of the reward that would have followed. The previous verse ended with the price the community paid for an art that could not profit it, and this sentence supplies the alternative it passed over. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the wish as a statement about what was available rather than a regret about what was impossible, which is the reading the grammar supports: the condition was within reach of the people being addressed. The method on display is the Book's habit of closing a section this way, describing a loss in terms of a choice that was open.

**FAITH AND MINDFULNESS NAMED TOGETHER**

The wish is completed by a second quality, and the two are joined in a single phrase: ***“and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah”***. Faithfulness and mindfulness are treated as the two halves of one posture, and the Book consistently pairs them when it describes what it means to hold a religion rather than to merely inherit one. The reward is described as better rather than large, which measures it against what the community actually received in the transaction just described. Someone who has been given a great deal and who has watched the same condition appear in the sources will recognise the comparison being drawn here. The sentence does not say the reward would have been infinite or immediate; it says it would have been better than the thing the buyers took instead, because the comparison being drawn is with the bargain the community actually struck.

**THE REWARD THAT WOULD HAVE FOLLOWED**

The phrase about the reward is placed where the reader expects a description of profit, and its wording is deliberately plain: what was on offer is named as a reward from Allah rather than as a technique, a status, or a possession. The contrast with the magic described in the preceding verse is exact, since that practice brought harm to its buyers while this reward is described from the hand of the One who gives it. The point of naming the giver rather than the gift is that the terms belong to the giver, and no resentment can alter them. Another sūrah states the rule this sentence assumes, and states it as a general law rather than a promise to one community: (16:96 — **“Whatever you have will end, but whatever Allah has is everlasting”**). The verse's wish is therefore about a durable return rather than a temporary advantage, and that contrast is the subject of the whole passage. A reader who measures his own choices by what lasts will find the comparison here easy to apply.

**A TRADER WHO KEEPS TWO SETS OF BOOKS**

Think of a trader who keeps two sets of books: the one he shows when he wants a quick return, and the one that would have grown quietly if he had credited it and left it alone. The community addressed here had a scheme beside it that cost more than it paid, and the verse names the alternative with the simplicity of a single word. The comparison is not between two equal offers; it is between something that ends and something that is described as coming from Allah, which places the two beyond any real competition. What turns on the comparison is the whole weight of the verse's regret, since the community is not accused of choosing a worse bargain by a small margin. Anyone who has watched a business kept alive for years on an arrangement everyone recognised as ruinous has seen the pattern, and the verse's regret is aimed at the recognition rather than the loss. What the sentence offers is the plain arithmetic of the choice.

**THE KNOWING THAT CHANGES NOTHING**

The verse ends where it began, with the same clause, and the repetition turns the wish into an assessment: ***“if only they knew”***. The Book has already stated, in the previous verse, that the buyers knew what they were taking on, so the closing clause is not a comment on missing information. It describes the gap between knowing a fact and letting the fact govern a decision, which is the subject the section has been building toward throughout. The clause is read by Ibn ʿAbbās as a statement about the community's knowledge of the scripture in its hands, and the reading fits the placement of the verse after the account of a covenant discarded and a Book cast away. What the reader carries away from the sentence is a question about whether his own conduct is governed by what he knows, and the question applies to the reader before it applies to anyone else.

---

## Verse 2:104

> O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!] But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!] and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment

**THE CONGREGATION TAKEN TO TASK**

The verse opens with a call to the believers, and the address establishes who is being corrected before the correction is stated: ***“O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.”*** ***“[Herd us!]”***. The instruction is given to the community that has accepted the message, which means the warning is not about an outsider's mockery but about a habit inside the household of faith. The word itself is an ordinary request in one language and an insult in another, and the translation supplies both meanings in brackets so that the reader can see the double edge. The Book's concern in the sentence is with what a community's speech signals about its stance, since the same request could be made with a word that carried no insult at all. What the reader is shown is a congregation being taught to weigh its words rather than to rely on its intentions.

**THE WORD THEY WERE TOLD TO DROP**

The first word is set aside in the same sentence that names its replacement, and the reason is the way it fell on the ear of the people being addressed. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās explains that the believers had taken up a form of address they had heard from the People of the Book, and that the form carried a jeer in the other community's usage. The verse does not require the believers to have intended the insult; it requires them to stop using a word that had become a mark of mockery in the mouths of others. This is the Book's consistent treatment of speech, since it judges what a phrase does in a community rather than what a speaker privately meant by it. A reader who has adopted the idiom of a hostile group without noticing what the idiom carries will find the instruction addressed to him.

**THE REPLACEMENT AND WHY IT WAS CHOSEN**
