The verse supplies the substitute immediately, and the substitute is a word that asks to be attended to: ***“But say, “Unẓurna,”*** ***“[Tend to us!]”***. The change is not a matter of taste; the second term asks for attention in a way that carries no hint of diminishment, which is what the first term had come to suggest. The Book's habit of replacing a defective practice with a sound one, rather than merely forbidding it, appears throughout this sūrah and is at work here in a single sentence. Another passage states the rule the verse applies, in the same four words it takes to give the instruction: (33:70 — **“Be mindful of Allah, and say what is right”**). A community's speech is treated as part of its obedience rather than as a private matter, and the verse's replacement shows how ordinary the corrected form was meant to be.

**A GUEST WHO COPIES THE WRONG PHRASE**

Think of a guest who copies a phrase he hears at a neighbour's table, not knowing that the phrase means something dismissive in the neighbour's own family. The community in this verse had been using the form with a decent intention, and the instruction came because the form itself had been turned against the faith. The account given in another passage describes the same practice from the other side, where the phrase is listed among the things said by a group that had made a game of the language: (4:46 — **“playing with words and discrediting the faith”**). What the verse corrects, then, is not a slip of the tongue but the acceptance of a vocabulary that had been fashioned to undermine the community that used it. A reader can carry the lesson to any idiom he has absorbed without asking what it was built to do.

**LISTENING AS PART OF SPEECH**

The instruction continues with a single imperative, and it is joined to everything that came before: ***“and listen ˹attentively˺.”***. The Book places hearing beside speaking, so that the corrected form is not enough by itself; a community that has been given a better word is also required to use its ears. The verse then names the consequence of refusing the whole matter, and the punishment is stated with the same brevity as the rest of the sentence: ***“And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment”***. The connection between mockery and disbelief is drawn by the verse rather than inferred by the reader, since the people who turned the greeting into a joke are named in the clause that follows. The duty to hear is placed on the community in another passage as well, where the listening is joined to the mercy that follows from it: (7:204 — **“listen to it attentively and be silent”**). What remains is the doubled instruction, one for the mouth and one for the ear, and the reader is left to take up both. The next verse explains why the hostility behind the mockery exists at all.

---

## Verse 2:105

> The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord, but Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty

**ENVY AT THE BLESSING OF OTHERS**

The verse turns from the corrected greeting to the resentment behind the mockery, and it names the parties without softening the description: ***“The disbelievers from the People of the Book”***. The Book has been speaking to the community that received the message, and here it explains that the objection to the message was never only about the wording used in the street. The party named first is the one that possessed scriptures of its own, which makes its resentment of a new blessing a matter of a different order from the ignorance of a people who had never received anything. Ibn ʿAbbās describes the verse as coming down over the leaders of that community and their refusal to see the Messenger's people favoured at all. What the reader is being prepared for is the reason behind the mockery, and the reason is named as a posture rather than an argument.

**DISBELIEVERS AND POLYTHEISTS MADE ONE PARTY**

The sentence joins a second party to the first, and the joining is itself a statement: ***“and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord”***. The two groups had little in common in their beliefs, and the Book places them together at the point where their attitude converges, which is the refusal to see the believers favoured. The blessing in question is from the Lord of the believers, so the refusal is directed at His choice rather than at their merit, and that is the subject of the sentence. The verse does not engage the objections of either group in detail here; it states the desire that stands behind them, and the statement is short because the desire is simple. A reader who has met hostility that could not be reasoned with has met the thing this clause describes, and the Book names it without pretending it is an argument.

**THE CHOICE THAT BELONGS TO ALLAH**

The next clause supplies the answer to the resentment, and it is an answer about authority rather than about merit: ***“but Allah selects whoever He wills”***. The verse does not argue that the believers deserved what they received; it places the giving where the Book always places it, in a choice that belongs to the giver. The same sentence reappears in another sūrah in nearly the same words, which shows how central the point is to the Book's treatment of favour: (3:74 — **“He chooses whoever He wills to receive His mercy”**). The resentment described in the earlier clauses is therefore a quarrel with a decision that was never submitted to the objectors in the first place. What the reader takes from the sentence is the ground of his own confidence, since a gift that depends on the giver's will is not diminished by anyone's disapproval.

**A DOOR NO ONE CAN SHUT**

Think of a house whose owner opens the door to a guest that the neighbours had decided to keep out, and who does not ask the neighbours for permission before doing it. The verse describes a favour that no amount of resentment could withhold, because the giving is placed in the hands of the One who owns the favour. The Book states the same position elsewhere when it discusses the bounty that passes between communities, and the verse here is one of its plainest statements of the principle. A reader who has been made to feel that his share of guidance was a matter for other people to approve has the sentence as his answer, and the answer is not a claim about his own worth. What is being refused in the earlier clauses is not the blessing but the freedom of the giver to bestow it.

**BOUNTY DESCRIBED AS A LORDLY ATTRIBUTE**

The verse closes by describing the One who gives, and the description is a statement about abundance rather than merely about power: ***“for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty”***. The word for bounty carries the sense of a giving that does not run down, which is why it is used to close a sentence about resentment over a gift. The sending of the Book is therefore presented as one instance of a generosity that has no narrow channel, and the verse intends the reader to see the objection as small beside the description that ends it. A community that reads the sūrah in order has already met this attribute in its opening verses, and the repetition at this point in the argument is deliberate. The same open-handedness is stated where the Book describes the reward of those who work: (24:38 — **“And Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit”**). The next verses answer a related objection, this time about what happens to earlier revelations when a new one arrives.

---

## Verse 2:106

> If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything

**WHAT ABROGATION MEANS IN THIS BOOK**

The verse takes up a question that had been raised against the revelation, and it answers it in the form of a law rather than a defence: ***“If We ever abrogate a verse”***. The Arabic term behind the translation carries the sense of lifting or transferring, and the Book uses it here for the withdrawal of a ruling by the One who gave it. The sentence is stated in the first person plural, which is the Book's usual manner when it describes acts it attributes to God, and the phrasing makes the whole matter an exercise of authority rather than an accident in the text. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās connects the verse to a specific objection from the People of the Book, who had asked why a ruling would be replaced if the earlier one had come from God. What the reader is offered is not an argument about the mechanics of revelation but a statement about who its author is.

**THE VERSE THAT IS REMEMBERED AND THE VERSE THAT IS REPLACED**

The sentence adds a second case to the first, and the second is the more striking of the two: ***“or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better”***. The forgetting here is attributed to the same authority that sends, which places the removal of a revelation within the same will as its delivery. The Book treats both cases identically in the sentence, and the equality is part of the answer, since the objection had been to replacement as such. The two cases are placed side by side because the will behind the sending is the same will behind the removal, which is the point the objectors had missed. The objection is not that something was lost but that something was changed, and the verse meets it by naming the one who does both. A reader who has wondered why the Book would speak of a verse passing out of memory has the sentence's own account of it here, and the account is short.

**BETTER AND SIMILAR, NOT LESSER**

The replacement is described in two words that between them close off every way of complaining about the change: ***“or similar one. Do you not know”***. The substitute is either better than what it replaces or equal to it, and the Book's choice of the two words rules out the complaint that something valuable had been taken away. What turns on the pairing is that no replacement can be described as a loss, which is why the sentence moves straight from the two words to the question that follows. Another sūrah records the same exchange from the side of those who refused it, and it supplies the accusation that was made against the one who brought the change: (16:101 — **“When We replace a verse with another”**). The sentence's own words then address the reader directly with a question, which moves the matter from a dispute about texts to the plainest available fact. The one who has followed the argument this far is asked to test the objection against what he already knows about the one who gives and withdraws.

**THE JEWISH OBJECTION THE SENTENCE ANSWERS**

The objection behind the verse was not a request for explanation; it was a use of the change as evidence against the mission. The Book meets it by refusing the premise, and the refusal is made in a sentence that never mentions the objectors, because the argument rests on a fact about God rather than on anything the objectors accept. What the verse assumes is that the right to revise a ruling belongs to the one who issued it, and that assumption is what makes the question that follows so pointed. The same line of reasoning appears elsewhere in the sūrah where the community's objections are answered by an appeal to divine prerogative rather than to the objector's satisfaction. Ibn ʿAbbās connects the verse with a challenge about the direction of prayer and similar changes, which puts it squarely among the objections the section has been addressing. A reader sees here how the Book handles a dispute it does not consider to be about evidence.

**CAPABILITY AS THE GROUND OF THE ANSWER**

The verse ends with a question about knowledge that is also a statement about power: ***“that Allah is Most Capable of everything”***. The clause gives the ground on which the whole answer rests, since a change of ruling is only a difficulty for someone who doubts the competence of the one who makes it. Capability is named here because the entire objection presupposes that a ruling was settled beyond revision, and the question leaves that presupposition with nowhere to stand. The Book frequently closes an argument in this way, and the closing here is deliberately placed after the objector has been asked twice whether he knows. Another passage states the same authority in terms of what is written and what is erased, which places the verse's own claim in the plainest company: (13:39 — **“Allah eliminates and confirms what He wills”**). What the reader carries away is a question addressed to himself, since the verse asks whether he has understood the position of the one whose words he is reading.

---

## Verse 2:107

> Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah, and you have no guardian or helper besides Allah

**DO YOU NOT KNOW, ASKED AGAIN**

The verse continues the questioning of the previous sentence and turns it toward the reader's own knowledge: ***“Do you not know”***. The repetition of the address is deliberate, since the Book is not asking for information but for attention to something the audience already holds. The question is placed before the content it introduces, so that the reader arrives at the statement that follows with the answer already half given. In the preceding verse the same phrasing introduced the claim about capability, and here it introduces a claim about ownership, which is the foundation the rest of the sentence rests on. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the two questions as one argument, the first about power over the revelation and the second about power over the order it addresses. What he is being asked to acknowledge is not a subtlety but the plainest fact the Book states about the world.

**THE KINGDOM THAT TAKES IN HEAVEN AND EARTH**

The question is followed by the statement it was preparing, and the statement moves from the heavens downward: ***“that the kingdom of the heavens”*** and then ***“and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah, and you have no guardian”***. The claim is one of ownership rather than of rule alone, and it covers both realms in a single sentence, so that nothing in the created order falls outside it. Another sūrah states the same fact in language close enough to serve as its witness, and it draws the same conclusion about protection: (9:116 — **“Indeed, to Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth”**). The Book's arguments about dependence repeatedly begin from this premise, and the verse here gives the reader the premise without ornament. A person who has accepted the opening of the sūrah has already accepted the sentence that follows from it.

**NO GUARDIAN AND NO HELPER BESIDE HIM**

The verse completes its claim with the human consequence, added to the ownership without a pause: ***“or helper besides Allah”***. The two terms name the two things a person in difficulty looks for, someone to take charge and someone to assist, and the sentence denies both outside the One who owns the kingdom. The clause is not a threat but a description, since a kingdom that is entirely owned leaves nothing and no one outside its owner's authority. The Book returns to this pair of words when it describes the condition of those who have no protector on the day the ownership becomes visible, and the vocabulary is consistent across the sūrah. A reader who has placed his confidence in a person or an institution has the sentence to reckon with, and the verse states the matter as something already known rather than as news.

**TRUST PLACED WHERE THE SENTENCE PLACES IT**

The sentence leaves the reader with a choice about where to put his reliance, and it does so by removing all the alternatives in one clause. The Book's treatment of trust follows the same pattern as its treatment of mercy in the earlier verse, where the giving is placed in the hands of the One who gives freely. The sentence never argues for reliance on God; it states the ownership, and the reliance follows from it as a conclusion. The Book's confidence in this method is visible throughout the sūrah, where statements about God's prerogative are used to settle disputes rather than to win them. A reader who has tried to hold the ownership of the heavens and the earth and the loyalty of his own heart at the same time will find the sentence's logic unavoidable. Another passage puts the conclusion in the mouth of the Prophet himself, and the words are the answer to the absence of any helper: (9:129 — **“Allah is sufficient for me”**).

**WHAT FOLLOWS FROM OWNERSHIP**

The verse closes the sequence that began with the objection to the believers' greeting, and it does so by returning the argument to its foundation. If the kingdom belongs to Allah, then the selection of whom to favour is His, the replacement of a verse is His, and the protection of a community is His. The question the verse asks is therefore a test of the reader's own position rather than a request for agreement, and the Book leaves it there. The next verses turn to what this community was told to do with the guidance it had been given, and the reader can follow the argument from ownership to obligation without a break in the reasoning. What the passage has established by this point is that the objections raised against the revelation were quarrels about a prerogative that was never delegated to the objectors at all.

---

## Verse 2:108

> Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger as Moses was asked before? But whoever trades belief for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way

**THE ADDRESS TURNED ON THE BELIEVERS**

The verse turns from the objections of the others to a question put to the believers themselves, and the question is about an appetite: ***“Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger”***. The address is startling because the community had just been defended against those who wanted to turn it back, and now it is asked whether it shares the very habit that made the others refuse. Nothing in the sentence claims that the believers had already asked anything; what is asked about is intention, and a question about intention is a warning rather than an accusation. The verse is attached by Ibn ʿAbbās to the Muslims in Medina, after some of them had begun to press the Prophet for the kind of signs their predecessors had demanded. The point of the question is to catch the desire at its root, because a community that copies the demands of an earlier people will eventually copy their conclusion as well.

**WHAT MOSES' PEOPLE HAD ASKED BEFORE**

The question is made concrete by a comparison with an earlier community: ***“as Moses was asked before?”***. The reference is to the demands recorded of the people who followed Moses, who asked to see God and asked for revelations in writing, and the Book treats the pattern as a familiar one rather than as an isolated incident. Another sūrah records the same demand being made to the Messenger in his own time, which shows how direct the likeness was: (4:153 — **“bring down for them a revelation in writing from heaven”**). The question in this verse therefore does not need to describe the earlier demands in detail, because the audience knew what had become of the community that made them. What the reader is asked to see is that the appetite for proof is not new, and that the Book's answer to it has been consistent from the beginning.

**THE INSTRUCTION ABOUT ASKING**

The comparison carries a warning that the verse states separately in another place, where the believers are told to leave certain questions alone: (5:101 — **“Do not ask about any matter which, if made clear to you, may disturb you”**). The Book's concern is not with curiosity as such but with the demand that God answer on the questioner's terms, which is what turned an earlier generation's request into a refusal. The verse assumes that a question can be an act of faith or an act of bargaining, and the difference lies in whether the questioner is prepared to accept the answer. A community that puts its confidence in the fact that the proof is available will not need to keep asking for more of it, because the point of asking has more to do with the asker than with the evidence.

**A CUSTOMER WHO KEEPS ASKING FOR SAMPLES**

Think of a buyer who asks for a sample of every item in a shop and never carries one home, and who eventually explains that he had no intention of buying. The people of Moses asked for signs and kept asking, and the Book records that the request did not improve their position; the verse asks the believers whether they intend to walk the same road. The comparison is uncomfortable because the motive in the shop is at least honest, whereas the demand for proof often dresses itself as a search for certainty. Someone who has watched a person demand more and more evidence before committing to anything has seen how the appetite works, and the verse's question is aimed at exactly that appetite. What the sentence offers as an alternative is the acceptance of a messenger, which is the thing the demands were designed to postpone.

**THE TRADE THAT ENDS IN STRAYING**

The verse closes by naming the outcome of the posture it has described, and it uses the language of commerce again: ***“But whoever trades belief”*** and ***“for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way”***. The metaphor of trade has run through this part of the sūrah, and the verb used here describes an exchange in which the better article is handed over for the worse. The clause about straying is the natural conclusion of the metaphor, since a person who has left the road is not one who is still examining the route. The verse therefore treats the persistent demand for proof as a transaction with a known price rather than as a neutral enquiry, and the reader is warned about the trade before he makes it. What remains with the reader is the question the verse opened with, now sharpened: what exactly does he intend when he asks for more than he has been given?

---

## Verse 2:109

> Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

**THE WISH HELD IN THE HEART OF THE OTHERS**

The verse names the desire behind the hostility the chapter has been describing, and it names the people it belongs to: ***“Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief”***. The wish is described as directed at a whole community rather than at an individual, and it is described as a wish rather than an attempt, which shows that the thing being reported here is an inner disposition. The Book has just finished answering the objections about abrogation and the choice of messengers, and it now identifies the source of the objections it has been meeting. The same aspiration is reported in another sūrah in almost the same terms, which shows that the verse is describing a settled attitude rather than a passing mood: (3:69 — **“Some of the People of the Book wish to mislead you”**). What the reader receives is a diagnosis, and the diagnosis is offered so that the community can meet the wish without being surprised by it.

**WHY THEY WANTED IT**

The motive is stated in the verse itself, and it is stated with a word that leaves no room for a generous reading: ***“because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon”***. The truth had been made clear to them, and the verse places that clause immediately before the command to pardon, so that the reader measures the offence in the light of what the offenders knew. The Book's treatment of envy here is consistent with its treatment elsewhere, where it asks the community to look at what has been given to others rather than at what it wishes for itself: (4:54 — **“Or do they envy the people for Allah’s bounties?”**). The desire to see the believers return to disbelief is not presented as a response to anything the believers had done; it is presented as resentment at a gift. A reader who has felt a similar pull when someone else received what he wanted will recognise the condition the verse is describing, and the recognition is not meant to be comfortable.

**THE COMMAND TO PARDON AND TO BEAR WITH THEM**

The next words are addressed to the community that had been wronged, and they are unexpectedly restrained: ***“and bear with them”***, followed by ***“until Allah delivers His decision.”***. The Book does not tell the community to argue down the envy or to answer it in kind; it tells the community to carry on with patience while the matter remains with God. The choice of patience rather than silence is significant, since the community is not asked to abandon its position but to hold it without retaliating. Ibn ʿAbbās is credited with dating the verse before the permission to fight, which would explain the direction given here, and the reading also fits the sequence of the sūrah. What the sentence asks of the believer is endurance of a specific kind, the kind that keeps its conduct unchanged while it waits.

**A NEIGHBOUR WHO WAITS FOR A TENANCY TO FAIL**

Think of a man whose neighbours would like him evicted, not because he has damaged anything but because they dislike the fact that he was given the house. The verse describes a community living beside people who wanted to see it fail, and the instruction given to the community is to keep living as it had been living. The Book's method here is to name the wish without making it the centre of the believer's attention, since a person who is always watching his envious neighbour will eventually imitate the behaviour he is watching for. Someone who has been made the object of dislike for the good that came to him will find the verse's counsel more useful than a strategy, because it removes the need to settle the account. What is left for the believer is the ordinary work of the community, carried on in the meantime.

**THE DECISION THAT BELONGS TO ALLAH**

The verse closes with the attribute that has ended several sentences in this stretch: ***“Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”***. The clause gives the community the reason it can wait, since the matter of who is favoured has already been shown to lie with the One who gives. The Book's habit of closing a command with a statement about God's capacity is a way of making the obedience reasonable rather than merely obligatory. What Ibn ʿAbbās hands down describes the warning here as one later answered by the command to fight and by the judgement that came upon the community that had chosen envy over the truth in front of it. A reader who has finished the sentence knows where the account will be settled, and the knowledge is the whole of the patience the verse asks for.

---

## Verse 2:110

> Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**THE WORK THE COMMUNITY IS TOLD TO DO**

After the envy and the command to wait, the verse gives the community something to occupy it, and the instruction is about practice rather than controversy: ***“Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth”***. The order of the sentence matters, since the Book answers the wish of the envious with a command about the believers' own conduct rather than with a rebuttal of the wish. Prayer and almsgiving are named together throughout this sūrah, which presents the two as one posture: worship directed upward and expenditure directed outward. The verse's placement after the report of hostility suggests that the community's best defence was never an argument but a pattern of life that could be seen. What the reader is given here is a way to spend the interval the previous verse described.

**THE FIGURE OF SENDING GOOD AHEAD**

The phrase about sending good ahead is a figure drawn from travel, and it describes goods dispatched before the traveller arrives: ***“for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do”***. The Book uses the figure to teach that the reward for a deed is not collected in the present but stored where the deed was sent, which is why the verse says the community will find it rather than receive it now. The plural form is used throughout the sentence, which places the responsibility on the community rather than on individuals alone, since prayer and almsgiving in the Book are gathered into the description of the believers as a body. Another sūrah joins the same practices to the same promise, which shows how stable the pairing is: (2:277 — **“Indeed, those who believe, do good, establish prayer, and pay alms-tax will receive their reward from their Lord”**). The verse therefore turns a report about other people's envy into an occasion for the believers' own accounting.

**THE EYES THAT SEE WHAT IS SENT**

The sentence ends with an attribute that answers a question the reader might not have asked aloud: if the reward is stored where the sender cannot see it, who keeps the record? The clause answers by naming God as All-Seeing of what the community does, which places the smallest deed inside a supervision that never lapses. The attribute also closes off the possibility that a good act might be lost through being unnoticed, since the Book treats the accounting as a matter of sight rather than of memory. The point of the clause is not that God is aware in general but that He is aware of this community's conduct in particular, and the verse places the two statements side by side without a connective. A reader who has given something quietly and wondered whether it counted has the sentence as the answer to his question, and the answer is stated before he asks it.

**A TRAVELLER WHO SENDS HIS LUGGAGE AHEAD**

Think of a traveller who sends his bags ahead to the city he is going to, so that he arrives without them and finds them waiting when he gets there. The verse uses the same logic for good deeds, and the travellers in the comparison are the believers who will one day arrive at the place where what they sent has been kept. The comparison also explains why the Book can call a deed an investment rather than a payment, since the reward is not presented as something received in exchange but as something restored to its owner. A reader who has experienced the ordinary truth that what is given away lasts longer than what is held will find the figure easy to carry, and the verse's instruction stands on that plain experience. What the sentence asks for is not a large gesture but a habit of sending, performed while the interval lasts.

**THE CLOSING ATTRIBUTE IN THIS VERSE**

The clause about sight has one more function in the passage, and it is aimed at the community's morale. The believers had been told to wait while others worked to turn them back, and a community in that position can easily conclude that its conduct is invisible and its patience unrewarded. The verse answers that conclusion by naming the One whose observation settles the account, and it places the answer at the end of a command rather than at the end of an argument. The Book's method in these verses is to move from what others wish to what the community does, and the movement is the whole of the answer. A reader who has kept to a practice he was told to keep and seen no return on it has the sentence as the statement he needs, and it is short enough to hold on to through the interval the verse has in view.

---

## Verse 2:111

> The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.”

**THE CLAIM THAT PARADISE BELONGS TO ONE COMMUNITY**

Two communities are reported here as holding a conviction about themselves, and the belief is stated plainly: ***“The Jews and Christians each claim that”*** ***“none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof”***. The Book joins the two communities in one sentence because the claim is formally the same on both sides, each excluding the other while using identical logic. The clause about desires comes before the invitation to bring proof, and its placement tells the reader that the Book is treating the belief as an expression of preference rather than as a conclusion drawn from evidence. The following verse supplies the answer, and this one prepares for it by asking the claimants to produce what they have. What the reader is watching is the Book's standard method with confident assertions: it asks for the document.

**A DESIRE NAMED AS A DESIRE**

The word used for the claim describes a wish rather than a judgement, and the choice of word does the work of an argument. A person who wants a conclusion to be true will often hold it with the confidence that belongs to a demonstrated fact, and the Book names the difference between the two. The claim is not answered by denying that its holders are sincere; it is answered by asking them to show that it rests on something outside their own wanting. Another sūrah states the same principle in the form of a direct correction, and its words are near enough to be the verse's own comment: (4:123 — **“neither by your wishes nor those of the People of the Book”**). A reader who has held a belief because it favoured his own community will find the sentence uncomfortably exact, and the exactness is the point of the verse.

**THE PROOF CALLED FOR AND WHAT IT WOULD BE**

The invitation to produce proof is phrased as a challenge rather than a request for a discussion, and its last clause qualifies the proof being asked for: ***“if what you say is true.”***. The qualification makes the demand reasonable, since a claim about the unseen can only be settled by a report from the One who knows the unseen. The Book does not ask the claimants to argue better; it asks them to demonstrate the authority behind a statement that no human being could otherwise make. The same standard is applied to the believers elsewhere in the sūrah, where their confidence is grounded in what has been sent down rather than in their own standing. The reading attached to Ibn ʿAbbās treats the proof being called for as the scripture already in the claimants' hands, which is why the correction that follows is not introduced as an argument. Anyone who has heard a person speak with certainty about who is saved and who is not will find the challenge useful, because it returns the matter to the only place where it can be settled.

**TWO FAMILIES DISPUTING AN INHERITANCE**

Think of two families who each insist that the estate belongs to them alone, neither of them able to produce the document that settles it. The two communities in this verse made the same claim about the inheritance of the world to come, and the Book asks both of them for the paper. The comparison is sharp because the claimants in it are not dishonest people; they are confident people, and confidence is easy to mistake for evidence. Someone who has seen a dispute run for years on nothing but the certainty of the parties can see how the Book wastes no time in choosing between them: it asks for the proof, and the absence of proof is the answer. What the verse leaves with the reader is a standard he can apply to his own convictions about who will be saved.

**WHAT REMAINS UNSETTLED HERE**

The verse does not name the answer to the claim, and that is deliberate, because the next verse supplies it in the Book's own words. What this sentence establishes is the common ground between the two claimants: both had a desire, both expressed it as doctrine, and neither could produce the authority they were asked for. The Book's order in the passage is worth noticing, since it lets the claimants state their case fully before it gives the correction that follows. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the sequence as a single argument in which the demand for proof and the answer that follows are two halves of one reply. Anyone who has followed the sūrah this far is now in a position to hear the correction as something more than a denial of two communities' hopes.

---

## Verse 2:112

> But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**THE CORRECTION THAT OPENS WITH A REFUSAL**

The claim of the previous sentence is met here, and the reply refuses the whole framing rather than adjusting it: ***“But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah”***. The refusal is aimed at the idea that salvation belongs to a community by name, and the sentence replaces the criterion with a description of a person. Submission and good conduct are named as the two marks of the one who has a reward with his Lord, and neither of them is an inherited identity. The Book's method here is to widen the door at the same moment that it removes the labels from it, which leaves the reader with a test he can apply to himself. What the previous verse asked the claimants to prove, this one answers by stating the condition on which the reward actually rests.

**SUBMISSION AND GOOD CONDUCT NAMED TOGETHER**

The two qualities are placed together because the Book does not recognise a submission that leaves conduct untouched, and the pairing is what turns a slogan about belonging into a description of a life. The word for submission carries the sense of handing over the whole self, and the good conduct that follows is the visible form of that handing over rather than a separate achievement. Another sūrah describes the same pair as a firm hold that a person can grasp, using language that fits this verse closely: (31:22 — **“Whoever fully submits themselves to Allah and is a good-doer”**). The sentence therefore states a condition that any person can meet, whatever community he was born into, which is why the refusal at its opening is followed by an invitation rather than by an exclusion. A reader who has been told that his standing depends on the group he belongs to will find the sentence's terms refreshingly ordinary.

**THE REWARD THAT BELONGS TO THE PERSON**

The next clause places the reward with the Lord rather than with the community: ***“and does good will have their reward with their Lord.”***. The Book consistently describes the reward as held by God rather than distributed by institutions, and the phrasing here removes every claim of ownership a community might assert over it. The same promise is made in the account of the believers, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians earlier in the sūrah, and the repetition of the terms there and here shows that the standard is not new: (2:62 — **“will have their reward with their Lord”**). What this sentence has accomplished, in two clauses, is to strip the claim of its exclusivity and to restate the condition in a form that applies to every human being. A reader who wants to know where he stands has the sentence's own criterion in front of him.

**AN ENTRANCE WITH NO GUEST LIST**

Think of a hall where the organisers had been arguing over whose names were on the list, and where the announcement comes instead that the door is open to anyone who meets the stated condition. The verse functions as that announcement, and it does so without naming the communities whose claims it has just refused. The comparison makes plain why the Book's answer is not a compromise between the two claimants, since neither is given what it wanted and both are offered the same terms. Anyone who has seen an argument about belonging collapse when the actual requirement is read out loud has seen the movement of this verse, and the movement is the Book's way of settling a dispute about privilege. What remains after the sentence is the condition itself, which each reader may test in his own life.

**THE FEAR AND THE GRIEF THAT ARE REMOVED**

The verse closes with a promise that appears in the Book when the reward has just been named, and it is stated twice in one sentence: ***“And there will be no fear”*** and then ***“for them, nor will they grieve”***. The two clauses remove the anxiety that belongs to the future and the sorrow that belongs to the past, which together cover the whole span of a person's worry. The Book uses the pair together here because the promise is being given to people who had been made anxious about their standing by the claims of others. The Book's habit of using these two words together makes the sentence a recognisable signature, and its appearance here ties the promise to the condition stated in the earlier clauses. The result is a verse that answers the claim of the previous sentence completely: it denies the exclusive reading, states the real condition, names where the reward is kept, and then takes away the two fears that motivated the dispute in the first place. A reader who has finished the sentence knows what is being asked of him and what he is being spared.

---

## Verse 2:113

> The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on” and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,” although both recite the Scriptures. And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺. Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute

**TWO CLAIMS MADE IN THE SAME BREATH**

A dispute between two communities that each held a scripture is reported here, with both positions set out side by side: ***“The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on”*** and ***“and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,”***. The symmetry is the point of the construction, since the Book puts the accusation and its mirror image side by side and lets the reader hear how they cancel each other. Neither claim is answered here with an argument about who is right, because the sentence is doing something else: it is showing that the two parties had made the same move against one another. The dispute had reached the believers as an invitation to take sides, and the Book's first response is to display the dispute for what it is. Anyone who has been drawn into a quarrel between two confident parties will recognise the pattern on display here.

**EACH SIDE ACCUSED OF HAVING NO GROUND**

The phrase translated as having nothing to stand on describes a position without a foundation, and each community applied it to the other while claiming the ground for itself. The Book has already described this community's habit of treating its own inheritance as the measure of everyone else, and the verse shows the same measure being used in the opposite direction. Another sūrah names the same dispute and gives its cause as envy rather than conviction: (3:19 — **“Those who were given the Scripture did not dispute ˹among themselves˺ out of mutual envy until knowledge came to them”**). The accusation in this verse is therefore not presented as the fruit of study, since each side was reading the same claim in the other's mouth. What the reader learns from the symmetry is that a quarrel conducted in these terms cannot produce a winner.

**SCRIBES WHO READ THE SAME BOOKS**

The verse then states the fact that makes the quarrel remarkable, and it states it briefly: ***“although both recite the Scriptures.”***. Both communities possessed and recited texts that they took to be from God, and the verse's clause places that shared practice beside the mutual accusation without comment. The contradiction is left to speak for itself here, since a person who recites a scripture and denies another community any ground occupies a position that the recitation will not support. The sentence does not say that the two scriptures were identical; it says that both parties were reciting, which is enough to show that the argument was not about information. A reader who has watched two people argue from the same document while each denies the other's reading of it has seen the condition the verse describes.

**THE PAGANS WHO REPEATED THE FORMULA**

The sentence widens to take in a third party, and the widening is a judgement on the first two: ***“And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺.”***. The people who had no scripture at all used the same formula as the communities who did, which means the formula belonged to a habit of mind rather than to a tradition. The Book's comparison is severe because it places the learned and the ignorant side by side on the strength of a shared sentence. What the verse establishes is that the denial of another person's ground is not produced by study, since the same denial appears where no study exists. Anyone who has heard a slogan repeated across very different groups will find the observation familiar.

**THE DAY THE DISPUTE IS SETTLED**

The verse closes by moving the dispute out of the community's hands and into a court that no party controls: ***“Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute”***. The same sentence is used elsewhere for the whole range of communities that disagreed about religion, and it is deliberately general: (22:17 — **“Allah will judge between them ˹all˺ on Judgment Day”**). The Book's answer to the quarrel is therefore not an adjudication in the present but a postponement to the day when the judgement is made by the One who knows what each community was given. The reader is left with the two claims ringing against one another and with a single sentence about the day they will be settled, a refusal to take the quarrel up on its own terms. What the passage requires of the believer is patience rather than a verdict, since the verdict has been reserved.

---

## Verse 2:114

> Who does more wrong than those who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship and strive to destroy them? Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear. For them is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter

**THE WORST WRONGDOING NAMED IN A QUESTION**

The verse opens with a question that measures a deed against every other deed, and it asks it in a form that expects no answer: ***“Who does more wrong than those”***. The Book uses this opening when it wants to place a piece of conduct beyond comparison, and the conduct here is not disbelief in the abstract but an act committed against a place and a name. The question is framed as a comparison, which means he is being asked to look for a worse offence and to find none. The verse's placement continues the sūrah's account of the communities that received scriptures, and it turns from their disputes to the harm some of them inflicted. What the reader is given first is a scale, and the deed is placed on it before it is described.

**THE NAME PREVENTED FROM BEING MENTIONED**

The deed is then spelled out, and its first part concerns speech: ***“who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship”***. The offence is not the neglect of worship by those who were charged with it; it is the active prevention of others from mentioning God where He is worshipped. The Book's attention to the divine name runs through the sūrah, and this verse treats access to it as a matter of right rather than of favour. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās connects the verse to the destruction of the sanctuary by a foreign power and to the obstruction the believers faced at the Sacred Mosque, which shows how the two halves of the deed belong together. The offence named first is an offence against speech, since the places are built for the mentioning of the name.

**STRIVING TO PULL THE PLACES DOWN**

The question adds a second charge to the first, and it escalates from obstruction to demolition: ***“and strive to destroy them?”***. The word for striving describes an effort that does not stop at a single act, which is why the verse attaches it to a campaign rather than an incident. The Book elsewhere describes the protection of houses of worship as a reason for the defence of a whole community, and it names the same kind of aggression in that connection: (22:40 — **“those who have been expelled from their homes for no reason”**). What the verse shows is that hostility to a place of worship is treated as hostility to what is mentioned in it, and the second charge therefore explains the first. Someone who has seen a community lose its place of gathering knows what the sentence is describing.

**ENTERING IN FEAR, OR NOT ENTERING**

The next clause states the consequence for the offenders, and it is phrased as a right that has been forfeited: ***“Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear.”***. The sentence does not describe a penalty imposed from outside; it describes the condition the offenders have brought on themselves, since a place they have attacked can no longer be a place of confidence for them. Another passage describes who is fit to maintain such places, and its answer turns on belief and conduct rather than on possession: (9:18 — **“The mosques of Allah should only be maintained by those who believe”**). The Book's logic here is that the guardianship of a sanctuary is a moral qualification rather than a legal title, and the verse's sentence removes both from those who fight it. A reader can see how the two communities that disputed in the previous verse are answered here by a standard about deeds.

**DISGRACE NOW AND PUNISHMENT LATER**

The verse closes by naming the two parts of the offender's lot, and it separates them by time and by severity: ***“For them is disgrace in this world”*** and ***“and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter”***. The pairing of an immediate shame with a deferred penalty is the Book's customary treatment of those who damage what belongs to God, and the same combination of the two outcomes appears in another passage about those who attack the community: (5:33 — **“This ˹penalty˺ is a disgrace for them in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter”**). The verse therefore does not leave the matter to the day the previous verse named; it states that the loss begins in the present, in the standing of those who act this way. The sentence shows the seriousness with which the Book treats the protection of worship, since it matches the offence with a loss in both worlds. The next verse turns from the attackers to the breadth of the One they were attacking, and it answers the restriction of worship to particular places.

---

## Verse 2:115

> To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah. Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing

**BOTH DIRECTIONS BELONG TO HIM**

The dispute about places and directions is settled here by removing the ownership of them from human hands, and the answer comes in the opening words: ***“To Allah belong the east”*** and ***“and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah. Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing”***. The two directions are named as a pair because they cover the whole compass between them, and the Book's point is that the owner of one half is the owner of the other. The previous verse had described people who tried to control where God's name is mentioned, and this one states who owns the space in question. The verse therefore answers the whole dispute about sanctuaries and orientations without mentioning either party to it. What the reader is offered is a fact about ownership rather than a ruling about a building.

**WHEREVER A PERSON TURNS**

The sentence draws a conclusion from the ownership, and the conclusion is stated without conditions: wherever the turning happens, the One being faced is Allah. The Book's phrasing is generous in its breadth, and the clause has been read by the early authorities in more than one setting: some reports tie it to a change of prayer direction, others to a prayer offered in the wrong direction by mistake. Ibn ʿAbbās is said to have connected the verse with a question the community raised about the earlier direction, and the answer given is about the One faced rather than about the wall faced. The sentence's purpose in the sūrah is to prevent a place from becoming a rival to the One who is worshipped in it, since a direction belongs to its owner as surely as the place does. A reader who has made a sacred thing out of a location will find the verse's correction in the clause about turning.

**THE OBJECTION ABOUT THE PRAYER DIRECTION**

The verse sits in a passage where the community's change of orientation had been raised by its critics, and the sentence supplies the ground on which such a change is no difficulty. Another sūrah records the same principle in a positive command, and its wording fits the situation this verse addresses: (2:148 — **“Everyone turns to their own direction ˹of prayer˺. So compete with one another in doing good”**). The Book's interest is in the competition of deeds rather than in the geography of prayer, and the sentence here states the reason that competition is possible: no direction is distant from its owner. The argument establishes that the dispute about orientation was never a dispute about access, since access has never depended on a wall.

**A MERCHANT WHO FINDS THE SAME OWNER EVERYWHERE**

Think of a traveller who looks for a particular merchant and discovers that every shop he enters belongs to the same man, so that no mistake about the address can keep them apart. The verse's claim about east and west works the same way, and it explains why the Book can treat a change of orientation as a small matter. The comparison also answers the resentment of the people described in the previous verse, since a person who owns the whole of a street cannot be shut out of part of it by anyone. Anyone who has feared that he was praying in the wrong place will find the sentence reassuring for the plainest reason, which is that the One addressed is not confined to the place. What the verse leaves the reader with is the freedom of the person who knows whose the ground is.

**ENCOMPASSING AND KNOWING**

The verse closes with two names that answer two different fears: the first answers the worry about being out of reach, and the second answers the worry about being unnoticed. The name translated as All-Encompassing describes a presence that no boundary can exclude, and the name that follows describes a knowledge that no hidden act escapes. The pairing is deliberate, because a person who is convinced that God is everywhere might still wonder whether his act in a strange place counts, and the second name settles that question. The Book frequently closes a statement about God's ownership with an attribute that covers the reader's practical worry, and the two words here do exactly that. What the sentence establishes is that the whole dispute about places was settled the moment its true owner was named, and the names that follow make the settlement personal.

---

## Verse 2:116

> They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him! In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth—all are subject to His Will

**AN OFFSPRING ATTRIBUTED TO GOD**

A claim about God is reported here that the Book treats as a category error rather than a difference of opinion, and it is stated in two words: ***“They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him!”***. The claim is quoted without its authors being named, which places the sentence beside the disputes of the earlier verses as one more assertion made about God without warrant. The Book's answer begins immediately with the words of exaltation rather than with an argument, and the order tells the reader that the claim is being refused at its root. The communities that made such claims had scriptures and traditions, and the verse shows the reader what can be said about God by people who have both. What follows in the sentence is the reasoning that the exaltation only begins.

**GLORY BE TO HIM AS THE ANSWER**

The phrase of exaltation is the Book's standard reply when a claim about God is too small for its subject, and its placement here is a judgement on the claim before any evidence is offered. The words describe God as free of every deficiency, and among the deficiencies is the suggestion that He shares His nature with anything. The Book uses the same phrase in other passages where the claim of offspring is reported, and in one of them the exaltation is followed by the same kind of reasoning used here: (19:35 — **“It is not for Allah to take a son!”**). The reader is therefore shown a pattern the Book follows consistently, where the claim is refused by a statement about what God is rather than by a comparison between God and the claimants. A person who has heard a doctrine about God that struck him as unworthy of the subject will recognise the reply.

**WHOSE THE HEAVENS AND THE EARTH ARE**

The verse then gives the reason the claim collapses, and the reason is about ownership: ***“In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens”***, ***“and the earth”*** and ***“all are subject to His Will”***. A person who owns everything cannot have derived a part of himself from it, since ownership and derivation are different relations and the verse keeps them apart. The same claim about ownership appears in a passage that also reports the claim of a son, and the order of the two statements there matches the order here: (6:101 — **“How could He have children when He has no mate?”**). The Book's argument is not that the claim is unlikely but that it is incoherent, since the one who owns all things has nothing beside Him from which anything could be begotten. The sentence therefore rests on a fact the reader has already met many times in the sūrah.

**A CRAFTSMAN WHO OWNS HIS WORK**

Think of a craftsman whose work fills a workshop and who is said to have fathered the furniture he made, so that the relation between him and his work is confused with the relation between him and a child. The verse's reasoning separates the two, and it does so by naming the whole created order as his possession. The comparison makes plain why the Book treats the claim as an error about God's nature rather than as an insult, since the mistake lies in the kind of relation that is being asserted. Anyone who has heard a person speak of the divine in terms drawn from human families can see how easily the confusion arises, and how simply the Book dissolves it. What the sentence leaves with the reader is the ownership of everything and the subordination of everything, which together rule out the claim.

**SUBJECTION AS THE STATE OF EVERYTHING**

The verse ends with a clause that goes beyond ownership to describe the condition of the created order: all are subject to His Will. The word describes a readiness to be directed, and it is applied here to everything in the heavens and the earth without exception. Closing a refutation with a statement about the created order shows the reader the scale of what is being discussed when a claim about God is made. The sentence declares God free of the deficiency, states that everything belongs to Him, and describes everything as under His command. The next verse names Him as the one who originated the heavens and the earth, which places the same reasoning in a sentence about creation itself.

---

## Verse 2:117

> ˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth! When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!” And it is

**THE ORIGINATOR NAMED FIRST**

The claim of the previous sentence is answered by naming God as the one who brought the heavens and the earth into being, and the name chosen describes invention rather than assembly: ***“˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens”*** and ***“and the earth!”***. The term used belongs to the vocabulary of creating something without a prior model, which is the answer to a claim about offspring in two ways: the originator is not the father of what he originates, and what he originates owes him everything. The Book's argument in the previous verse rested on ownership, and this sentence supplies the ground of that ownership by naming the act that produced it. A reader who has followed the sequence has now been given the reason the claim cannot stand, and the reason is the relation between a maker and what he makes. What the reader receives here is a title rather than an argument, and the title settles the matter.

**DECREE DESCRIBED IN A SINGLE WORD**

The sentence then describes how this originator acts when he decides something: ***“When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!”***. The contrast with the claim of the previous verse is exact, since the Book has just denied that God has offspring and now shows how everything that exists came to be: by a command. No intermediary, no partner and no material is named, and the absence is the whole content of the clause. Another sūrah states the same principle in similar words, and it also draws the conclusion that a child is impossible for such a maker: (40:68 — **“When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it”**). The Book uses this sentence wherever it needs to establish that creation depends on God's word alone, which is why it appears in the answers to several claims about divine sonship. A reader who has understood the clause has understood why the claim of the previous verse could not survive.

**BE, AND IT IS**

The command is quoted in the verse itself, and the sentence closes with the result following immediately on the word: ***“And it is”***. The Book places no interval between the decree and the existence of what is decreed, and the two words that end the sentence carry the whole of its force. The same pair of words describes the coming into being of a child in the annunciation to Mary, where the impossibility is answered in exactly this form. The use of so short a sentence for so large a claim is deliberate, since the Book's manner in these verses is to state the ease of the act rather than to describe its mechanics. The picture left behind is one of a command that is not followed by effort.

**A BUILDER WHO SPEAKS THE HOUSE INTO PLACE**

Think of a builder who does not lay a single brick but describes a house and finds it standing where he spoke of it. The verse's clause about the decree works at a larger scale and with no comparison intended, since the point of the image is that the result has no relation to labour. The comparison also makes clear why the two sentences of this passage belong together: the one denies that God has a family, and the other shows that what exists came to be without the involvement that a family would imply. Anyone who has watched a person try to account for the world without a maker can see how much the Book's answer depends on this single clause. What the verse offers is not an explanation of creation but the plainest statement of who created.

**THE PAIR OF VERSES AND WHAT THEY SETTLE**

Read together, the two sentences answer the claim of offspring in two stages, and each stage removes a different part of it. The ownership of everything rules out the possibility of a derived divine nature, and the command that produces everything rules out the need for any such derivation in the first place. The Book's practice in these verses is to answer a doctrinal claim with a statement about God's relation to the created order, and the two statements here are as brief as any in the sūrah. A reader who wanted a longer argument has the short one to work with, since the sentence about the decree leaves nothing for a partner to do. What remains for the reader is the title with which the passage opened, and the ease with which the Book has disposed of the claim.

---

## Verse 2:118

> Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us or a sign would come to us!” The same was said by those who came before. Their hearts are all alike. Indeed, We have made the signs clear for people of sure faith

**THE DEMAND TO HEAR GOD SPEAK**

The verse puts a demand into the mouths of the people who had no scripture, and it quotes them directly: ***“Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us”*** and ***“or a sign would come to us!”***. The demand is not for a clearer argument but for a different kind of communication, one in which the audience sets the terms. The Book has spent several verses answering claims made by communities with scriptures, and it now turns to the party that had no book at all and shows that the same demand was in its mouth. The phrasing is important because it places the condition on God rather than on the hearers, as though the message could only be accepted if it arrived by the route they had chosen. The demand on display is one that would not have settled anything, since it asks for a sign whose terms are dictated by the people who would have to accept it.

**THE OLD DEMAND IN NEW MOUTHS**

The sentence then connects the demand to an older history, and the connection is the answer: ***“The same was said by those”*** and ***“who came before. Their hearts are all alike.”***. The Book's argument is about resemblance rather than about chronology, and the clause about the hearts states the reason the same words keep appearing in different centuries. Another sūrah records the demand in the mouth of the community that received Moses, where the request for a sign was followed by the same refusal as before: (6:124 — **“We will never believe until we receive what Allah’s messengers received”**). The repetition is offered as evidence that the demand does not arise from the case being made but from a condition of the heart, and the sentence states that condition in four words. Anyone who has watched the same objection surface in every generation has the sentence to explain it.

**HEARTS THAT CAME OUT ALIKE**

The clause about the hearts is the hinge of the verse, because it moves the discussion from the evidence to the people who are examining it. The Book treats the heart as the place where a decision about a message is taken, and sameness of heart explains the repetition of speech. Another passage records the demand as it was made to Moses' community, and it shows how quickly a request for direct communication turns into a rehearsal of an old complaint: (10:20 — **“Why has no ˹other˺ sign been sent down to him from his Lord?”**). The sentence's refusal to describe the demanders as stupid is notable, since it places the problem in a disposition rather than in an intellect. Someone who recognises his own capacity for that disposition will find the clause more useful than an insult would have been.

**A WELL THAT TASTES THE SAME IN EVERY VILLAGE**

Think of a family that has moved through four different towns and found the water in each of them bitter, and that blames the towns. The verse tells the reader that the same complaint has been made in every generation, and it places the cause in the hearts that carried the complaint from place to place. The comparison also illuminates why the Book does not answer the demand with a demonstration, since a demonstration is what the demanders asked for and did not want. Anyone who has watched a person find fault with every alternative he is offered can see the pattern the sentence describes, and the pattern is not about the alternatives. The point is that the issue has never been the availability of the signs.

**THE SIGNS MADE CLEAR FOR THE SURE**

The verse closes by stating what has been provided instead, and the statement is unqualified: ***“Indeed, We have made the signs clear”*** and ***“for people of sure faith”***. The signs are described as clear without a condition, and the qualification falls on the people to whom they are clear, which places the difficulty on the receiving side. The particular phrase used here for sure faith describes a confidence that does not wait for further evidence, and the Book treats that confidence as the condition of seeing what is already there. Another sūrah makes the same link between the clarity of the revelation and the people who recognise it: (45:20 — **“a guide and mercy for people of sure faith”**). The sūrah has used this contrast from its opening verses, where the same clarity is placed against the same kind of heart, and the verse here repeats the pattern at the close of an argument. What remains with the reader is the offer of the signs and the phrase that describes those who see them.

---

## Verse 2:119

> We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺ as a deliverer of good news and a warner. And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire

**THE TRUTH THE MESSENGER WAS SENT WITH**

The attention moves from the demands of the audience to the description of the one who brought the message, and his commission is stated in three parts: ***“We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺”***, ***“as a deliverer of good news”*** and ***“and a warner.”***. The truth is named as what the sending carried, which places the message rather than the messenger's person at the centre of the sentence. The two roles that follow describe what the truth does when it reaches people: it announces something to those who accept it and warns those who do not. The preceding sentence has just described an audience whose hearts all came out alike, and this sentence answers that scene by describing the work that continues regardless. What the reader receives is a picture of a mission that does not depend on the response it meets.

**GOOD NEWS AND WARNING AS ONE OFFICE**

The pairing of the two roles is not a division of labour between two messengers but a description of a single office, and the Book uses the pair together whenever it summarises a prophet's work. The good news comes first, which is worth noticing, since the warning is not the whole of what the messenger carries or even most of it. Another sūrah makes the same point when it lists what the earlier messengers brought and what they met: (3:184 — **“so too were messengers before you who came with clear proofs”**). The Book's habit of naming both roles together is a way of saying that the message is complete in what it offers and complete in what it threatens, so that no hearer can claim he was told only half. A reader who has heard the message described only as judgement will find the order of the words here worth his attention.

**THE MESSENGER NOT ANSWERABLE FOR THE OTHERS**

The sentence then relieves the messenger of a burden that the previous verses could easily have placed on him: ***“And you will not be accountable”*** and ***“for the residents of the Hellfire”***. The Book states this as a fact about the mission rather than as a comfort offered to a discouraged man, and the statement follows the description of the office directly. The same assurance appears in the history of the earlier messengers, whose audiences mocked them while the messengers delivered what they had been given: (36:30 — **“No messenger ever came to them without being mocked”**). The division of responsibility runs between the delivery and the response, and only the first belongs to the messenger. A reader who carries a message to people who will not hear it has the sentence as the limit of his obligation.

**A HERALD WHO DOES NOT OWE THE CITY ITS ANSWER**

Think of a herald who rides through a town reading the proclamation and who is not asked afterwards whether the townspeople agreed with it. The verse describes the prophet's work in the same terms, and it names the two directions the proclamation can take without making either of them the messenger's responsibility. The comparison is useful because the pressure a messenger feels is usually about results, and the sentence here removes results from the account. Anyone who has tried to make another person believe something for his own good knows the exhaustion the verse is lifting, and the lifting is done in a single clause. What remains with the messenger is the delivery, which is the part he was given to do.

**THE DELIVERY AND THE RESPONSE**

Read with the verses around it, this sentence explains why the Book can describe an audience that refused and still call the sending a sending. The signs were made clear for people of sure faith, the demand for a different kind of proof was refused, and the messenger is told that the residents of the Fire are not his to answer for. The three statements together form the answer to the objection recorded in the previous verse, and the answer is about the nature of the mission rather than about the objectors' standing. The Book's restraint here is part of its method, since it leaves the outcome with God and the delivery with the messenger. Anyone who has wondered how a prophet could continue after so much refusal has the sentence as the Book's own account of it.

---

## Verse 2:120

> Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah

**A SATISFACTION THAT WILL NEVER COME**

The verse states a limit that the community had to accept, and it states it in the form of a prediction: ***“Never will the Jews”*** and ***“or Christians be pleased with you”***, followed by ***“until you follow their faith.”***. The two communities are named together again, as they were in the dispute over Paradise, and the sentence explains an experience the believers had been living through. The Book's wording is absolute, and the condition attached to it shows what would have been required: not better conduct, not clearer argument, but the adoption of the others' religion. The sentence is therefore a description of the terms rather than a complaint about the parties, and the terms are of a kind that a believing community cannot meet. What the sentence removes is the expectation that a certain kind of effort will eventually produce approval.

**THE GUIDANCE NAMED AS ALLAH'S OWN**

The verse supplies the reply the Messenger is to give, and the reply declines the offered terms by naming what he already has: ***“Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.”*** and ***“And”***. The sentence does not enter into a comparison between the two faiths; it states that guidance is a gift from God rather than a possession of a community. The same phrase appears elsewhere in the Book where the claim of belonging is being corrected, which shows how fixed the formula was: (3:73 — **“Surely, ˹the only˺ true guidance is Allah’s guidance”**). Placing this statement immediately after the prediction gives the reader the reason the community could not be satisfied by anything short of conversion: what was at stake was not the approval of the neighbours but the source of the guidance itself. A reader who has been asked to soften a position merely to keep the peace will recognise the reply.

**THE DESIRES THAT WOULD LEAD AWAY**

The verse then addresses a possibility that would never have arisen in a straightforward reading, and it warns against it in the strongest form: ***“if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge”***, ***“that has come to you, there would be none to protect”*** and ***“or help you against Allah”***. The warning is given to the Messenger, which addresses the community that follows him, and the words carry the weight of the whole sūrah's argument about what has been received. Another passage states the same danger in a general form, where obedience to the majority is shown to lead away from the path: (6:116 — **“If you were to obey most of those on earth, they would lead you away from Allah’s Way”**). What the Book says about the pressure to conform does not change here, since the danger it names is the desires of other people rather than their arguments.

**TWO HOUSES AND A FENCE THAT CANNOT BE MOVED**

Think of a household whose neighbours will not be satisfied until it moves in with them, and which is asked to give up its kitchen to keep the street quiet. The verse describes a demand of that shape, and it refuses the concession without pretending that the neighbours will change their minds. The comparison is useful because it separates two things a reader easily confuses: being pleasant to one's neighbours and being absorbed by them. Anyone who has seen a conviction given up in small instalments to keep a relationship calm can see what the warning is aimed at, and the warning is not about hostility but about drift. What the verse leaves with the reader is the knowledge of what the pressure is for.

**WHAT REMAINS AFTER THE REFUSAL**

The verse ends with the removal of every other protector, so that the community is left with no fallback if it yields. The sūrah has already spoken of the east and the west belonging to God, and the same ownership is stated here as the reason no help exists outside Him. The sentence therefore closes the discussion of the neighbours' approval by placing the community's security entirely with God, which is the answer to the fear that refusing them would leave the believers alone. A reader who has taken the sentence seriously knows what he is choosing when he keeps a conviction under pressure, and he knows whom he is choosing instead. The next verse describes the community that had received the same scripture and held to it, which supplies the contrast the passage has been building.

---

## Verse 2:121

> Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it. As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers

**THE PEOPLE WHO FOLLOW THE BOOK AS IT SHOULD BE FOLLOWED**

The verse describes a group inside the communities that possessed scriptures, and it does so by what they do rather than by what they are called: ***“Those We have given the Book follow it”*** and ***“as it should be followed. It is they”*** who ***“who ˹truly˺ believe in it.”***. The phrase about following as it should be followed describes a manner of reading rather than a quantity of reading, and the Book's wording makes the manner the standard. The verses just before this one described communities that would not be satisfied until the believers joined them, and this sentence points to the people within those same communities who had done the opposite. The verse therefore prevents the reader from turning the previous sentence into a verdict on everyone who inherited a scripture. What the reader is given is a description that any holder of a book can test himself against.

**FOLLOWING A BOOK PROPERLY**

The Book's understanding of following is practical rather than ceremonial, and the verse's two-word standard leaves the reader to work out what it involves. A book is followed properly when its commands are carried out, its warnings are taken seriously, and its claims are not reshaped to fit the reader's preferences. Earlier verses in this passage described communities that recited their scriptures while hiding what they contained, and the contrast here is with people who read and comply. Another passage describes the same group in terms of their conduct at night, which gives the reader a picture of what the phrase looks like in a life: (3:113 — **“Yet they are not all alike: there are some among the People of the Book who are upright”**). The point is that the failure described earlier in the sūrah was never a failure of access to the text.
